react-q1.testing: whether you name the programming-model change, not "the virtual DOM".
react-q1.trap: "React is fast because of the virtual DOM."
react-q1.spoken:
"React turns UI into a function of state. I describe what the screen should look like for the current data, and React works out how to get the DOM from the old state to the new one. With hand-written DOM code, I own every transition — add this class, remove that node, update this counter in three places — and that's where the bugs live: two places disagree about what the screen should be.

The unit of reuse is the component: markup, behaviour and local state together, composed like functions.

The price is an abstraction layer, a runtime in the bundle, and a re-render model I now have to reason about — when things render, and why."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: UI as a function of state
stages.html: "UI = f(state): I write the target, React computes the transition."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
Prove it — the same feature, imperative vs declarative:

// Imperative: every transition by hand; easy to forget one
button.onclick = () => { count++; label.textContent = count; if (count > 9) badge.classList.add('hot') }

// Declarative: describe the result; React applies the diff
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)
  return <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>{count}{count > 9 && <b>hot</b>}</button>
}
  • Imperative: reset, undo or a second button changing count each need matching DOM code. Declarative: every path goes through state.

stages.name: What it costs
stages.claim: a model to learn and a runtime to ship
stages.html:
Cost Detail
bundle React + ReactDOM runtime (tens of KB gzipped)
mental model render vs commit, identity, stale closures, effects
performance traps unnecessary re-renders, effect waterfalls

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html: • Complex forms, dashboards and streaming chat UIs where many inputs affect one screen: one source of truth, many derived views.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • The follow-up is always "what happens between setState and the pixel?" (Q3).

followUps.question: 🧪 A counter is shown in the header and in a sidebar badge. Imperatively, what goes wrong when you add a reset button?
followUps.html: The reset handler must update both DOM places; forget one and they disagree. Declaratively both read the same state, so reset is one setCount(0).

followUps.question: "React is fast because of the virtual DOM."
followUps.html: The virtual DOM is overhead React pays to let you write declaratively. It's fast enough, not faster than well-written direct DOM code (Q6).

followUps.question: What's a component, really?
followUps.html: A function from props (and its own state) to a description of UI. React calls it; you never call it directly.

followUps.question: When would you not use React?
followUps.html: Mostly static content (plain HTML or a static site generator), tiny widgets where a runtime isn't worth it, or performance-extreme canvases where you draw directly.

followUps.question: For an AI chat product, what does the model buy you?
followUps.html: Messages, streaming state, tool-call traces and errors live in state; the screen follows. Retry, edit and regenerate become state transitions rather than DOM surgery — which is where chat UIs usually break.

dontSay: A tour of features instead of the model.

react-q2.testing: state as a per-render snapshot, and queued updates.
react-q2.trap: answering 3 because "setCount is called three times".
react-q2.spoken:
"It shows 1.

State is a snapshot per render. When the click handler runs, count is the value from the render that created the handler: zero. So all three calls compute 0 + 1 and each queues 'set count to 1'. React batches them into one re-render, and the last value wins: 1.

If I want three increments, I use the updater form, setCount(c => c + 1). Updaters are queued and each receives the result of the previous one, so they compute 1, 2, 3.

The rule of thumb: if the next state depends on the previous state, use the updater."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  const handleClick = () => {
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
    setCount(count + 1);
  };
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{count}</button>;
}
  • A: 3 · B: 1 · C: 0 · D: 2

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.claim: three writes of the same value
stages.html:
Call count read Queued update
1 0 set to 1
2 0 set to 1
3 0 set to 1
re-render — count = 1

Prove it:

// click once, then read the button
// → "1"   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
// with setCount(c => c + 1) ×3
// → "3"

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
• Each render has its own count constant; handlers close over it (a JavaScript closure, not React magic).
  • setX(value) queues a replacement; setX(fn) queues a function applied to the pending state.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Result
three setCount(c => c + 1) 3
setCount(count + 1) then setCount(c => c + 1) 2
setCount(c => c + 1) then setCount(count + 1) 1
console.log(count) after the calls logs 0 (snapshot)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Likes, quantity steppers, "load more" counters: rapid clicks or async callbacks using the snapshot lose updates. Updater form everywhere the next value depends on the previous one; useReducer when several fields change together.

followUps.question: setCount(count + 1); setCount(c => c + 1) — what renders?
followUps.html: 1. The first queues "set to 1"; the updater then receives 1 and returns 2.

followUps.question: "setState is async, that's why."
followUps.html: Imprecise. The real reason is that count is a constant from the current render; even synchronous updates wouldn't change that variable inside the running handler.

followUps.question: How many re-renders does one click cause?
followUps.html: One: the three updates are batched inside the event handler (and everywhere since React 18).

followUps.question: When is setCount(count + 1) fine?
followUps.html: When it's the only update in the handler and nothing async sits between reading and writing. The updater is still the safer default for derived-from-previous values.

followUps.question: A cart quantity stepper loses clicks under a slow network. Why and fix?
followUps.html: Handlers or async callbacks compute from a stale snapshot. Use updaters for local state, send the intended delta or final value to the server with idempotency, and reconcile the server response (Q26).

react-q3.testing: schedule → render (pure, interruptible) → commit (atomic) → layout effects → paint → passive effects.
react-q3.trap: "React updates the DOM when you call setState."
react-q3.spoken:
"Calling setState doesn't touch the DOM. It enqueues an update on that component's fiber with a priority — a click is urgent, a transition is not — and schedules work.

Then the render phase: React calls the component functions that need re-rendering, starting from the updated component and going down its subtree, and builds a new tree of elements. It compares it with the previous one — reconciliation — to work out what changed. This phase must be pure: no DOM writes, no side effects, because in concurrent rendering React can pause it, throw it away, or render twice in development.

Then the commit phase, which is synchronous and atomic: React applies all the DOM mutations at once, attaches refs, and runs layout effects — useLayoutEffect — before the browser paints, so measurements there can still change what's shown without a flicker.

Then the browser does style, layout and paint: the pixel changes.

Finally passive effects — useEffect — run after paint, so they don't block the frame.

That split explains most performance advice: keep render cheap and pure, keep layout effects rare, and put side effects in useEffect."

stages.name: The one-line claim
What React does
stages.html:
Phase Work Can be interrupted?
schedule queue update with a lane (priority), batch —
render call components, reconcile children yes (concurrent)
commit mutate DOM, set refs, layout effects no
paint browser —
passive effects useEffect callbacks and cleanups runs after paint

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
function Demo() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0)
  console.log('render', n)
  useLayoutEffect(() => console.log('layout effect', n))
  useEffect(() => console.log('effect', n))
  return <button onClick={() => setN(1)}>{n}</button>
}
// after one click (no StrictMode):
// → render 1 · layout effect 1 · effect 1     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

Development StrictMode adds a second render and effect pass on mount (Q12).

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.claim: impure render and heavy layout effects
stages.html:
Mistake Effect
side effects in render duplicated or lost in concurrent/StrictMode renders
heavy work in render slow commits, poor INP
measuring DOM in useEffect a visible flicker (use layout effect)
heavy useLayoutEffect blocks paint

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html:
• 18: concurrent rendering (interruptible render phase), automatic batching everywhere, transitions.
  • 19: Actions, use, and the React Compiler (optional) reducing re-render work.

followUps.question: You call setN(1) and then console.log(ref.current.textContent) in the same handler. What does it log?
followUps.html: The old value: the DOM hasn't been committed yet. Read it in an effect after commit, or use flushSync to force a synchronous commit (rarely justified).

followUps.question: "The virtual DOM diff is what makes updates expensive."
followUps.html: Usually the cost is re-running component functions (render work) and whatever they compute, not the diff itself. Profile to see where commit time goes.

followUps.question: Why must render be pure?
followUps.html: React may render a component, pause, discard the result and render again (concurrency, StrictMode, Suspense). Side effects in render would run the wrong number of times.

followUps.question: What does a "lane" mean?
followUps.html: A priority bucket for updates; urgent input goes in a sync/default lane, transitions in a lower one, so React can render urgent updates first (Q35).

followUps.question: INP is poor on a filter page. How does this model guide you?
followUps.html: Measure where the interaction's time goes: long render (too many components, heavy calculations → move state down, memo, transitions), long commit (huge DOM → virtualise), or long effects blocking. The fix differs per phase (Q29, Q34).

react-q4.testing: the two heuristics (type and key) and identity-based state preservation.
react-q4.trap: "keys are for performance" or "keys just silence a warning".
react-q4.spoken:
"Reconciliation is how React turns a new element tree into DOM updates. A general tree diff is far too expensive, so React uses two heuristics that make it linear.

First, type: if an element at the same position has a different type — a div becomes a span, or Profile becomes Login — React throws away the old subtree, including all its state, and mounts a new one. Same type: React keeps the instance and updates its props.

Second, keys for lists: among siblings, React matches old and new children by key rather than by position. So when an item moves, React moves the existing instance — its state, its DOM, its focus — instead of updating every row with its neighbour's data.

So a key is identity. It tells React which component instance is which across renders. That's also why a key can deliberately reset a component: give it a new key and React sees a different instance, unmounts the old one and mounts a fresh one.

The rule: keys must be stable and unique among siblings — usually a database ID. Array indexes are only safe if the list never reorders, inserts or deletes."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: type decides remount, key decides identity
stages.html: "Same type at the same slot → update; different type → remount; in lists, the key is the slot."

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
Situation React's action
same type, same position keep instance, update props
different type unmount subtree (state lost), mount new
list children with keys match by key; move, insert, remove
list children without keys match by index (warning)
key changes on one element treated as a new instance: remount

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: state follows the key, not the position
stages.html:
function Row({ label }) { return <li><span>{label}</span><input defaultValue={label + '-note'} /></li> }
function List({ items, byIndex }) { return <ul>{items.map((it, i) => <Row key={byIndex ? i : it} label={it} />)}</ul> }
// render ['a','b','c'], then ['b','c'] (delete 'a'); read label:input per row
// → key=index  b:a-note c:b-note     (inputs kept their old rows' values)
// → key=id     b:b-note c:c-note     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.claim: index keys, random keys, reused slots
stages.html:
• Index keys on editable or reorderable lists (Q5).
  • Random keys (Math.random()) → every render remounts everything: lost state, slow.
  • Same component type swapped conditionally at the same slot keeps state you expected to reset (Q30 — fix with a key).

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html: • The heuristics have been stable since React 16 (Fiber). React 19 adds nothing new here; the React Compiler doesn't change identity rules.

followUps.question: {isAdmin ? <Panel /> : <Panel />} — does toggling isAdmin reset Panel's state?
followUps.html: No: same type at the same position, so React keeps the instance. Add key={isAdmin ? 'admin' : 'user'} to force a reset.

followUps.question: "Keys are a performance optimisation."
followUps.html: They're about correctness first: which instance keeps which state. Performance (moving instead of re-creating) follows.

followUps.question: Why not do a full tree diff?
followUps.html: Optimal tree edit distance is roughly O(n³); React's heuristics make it O(n), which works because UIs rarely move subtrees across levels.

followUps.question: Do keys need to be globally unique?
followUps.html: Only among siblings in the same list.

followUps.question: Where have you used a key deliberately?
followUps.html: To reset a form or editor when the selected record changes (key={recordId}), avoiding an effect that manually clears state — cleaner and bug-free (Q30).

react-q5.testing: index keys encode position, not identity, so state stays at the position.
react-q5.trap: blaming the form library or the state update.
react-q5.spoken:
"Index keys tell React that a row's identity is its position. When the first row is deleted, the item that was at index 1 is now at index 0, so React matches it with the old component at key 0 — the one that belonged to the deleted row — and just passes it new props.

Anything that isn't driven by props stays behind: useState inside the row, and uncontrolled DOM state like an input's typed value, focus or scroll position. So the labels update correctly, but each input still shows the value typed into the row that used to be in that position. The last component, key 2, is the one that gets unmounted.

The fix is a stable key from the data — key={item.id} — so React knows the second item's component moves up rather than being reused. If items don't have IDs, I generate one when the item is created, not during render."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html: • Prop-driven text updates; component state and DOM state (uncontrolled inputs, focus) don't.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.claim: reproduce with a delete in the middle
stages.html: • Delete the first row and compare each row's label with its input. The mismatch shifts by one row.

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Tell
index keys mismatch appears exactly after insert/delete/reorder
missing keys (defaults to index) same, with a console warning
random keys inputs lose focus and reset every render
state stored per position in a parent array same symptom, data-level

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it:

function Row({ label }) { return <li><span>{label}</span><input defaultValue={label + '-note'} /></li> }
function List({ items, byIndex }) { return <ul>{items.map((it, i) => <Row key={byIndex ? i : it} label={it} />)}</ul> }
// render ['a','b','c'], then ['b','c']
// → key=index  b:a-note c:b-note
// → key=id     b:b-note c:c-note     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
• key={item.id}; for client-created rows, assign crypto.randomUUID() when the row is created and store it with the item.
  • Prefer controlled inputs whose value lives with the item, so data and UI can't drift.

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.claim: a lint rule and a delete-a-row test
stages.html: • Lint rule react/no-array-index-key; a test that deletes a middle row and asserts each input's value.

followUps.question: 🧪 Same list, but rows only display text (no inputs, no state). Any visible bug with index keys?
followUps.html: No visible bug: every row is fully prop-driven, so the reused components just get new props. It's slower for large lists (every row updates) but correct.

followUps.question: "Index keys are fine because the warning goes away."
followUps.html: The warning disappears, the bug doesn't. Index keys are only safe for static lists that never reorder, insert or delete.

followUps.question: Why is key={Math.random()} worse?
followUps.html: Every render produces new keys, so every row remounts: state lost, focus lost, and a lot of extra work.

followUps.question: Does React.memo help here?
followUps.html: No. Memo skips re-renders; it doesn't change which instance matches which item.

followUps.question: A drag-and-drop list of editable cards has this bug in production. How do you fix it safely?
followUps.html: Switch to stable IDs, add a regression test for reorder and delete, and check any per-row state stored in parent arrays by index — migrate it to maps keyed by ID.

react-q6.testing: honesty about overhead, and knowing what the virtual DOM is actually for.
react-q6.trap: "Yes, the virtual DOM makes React fast."
react-q6.spoken:
"No. The virtual DOM is extra work on top of the DOM updates you'd do anyway: React builds a description of the UI, compares it with the previous one, then applies the same DOM changes a careful hand-written update would apply. So for any single update, optimal direct DOM code is at least as fast.

What the virtual DOM buys is a declarative model that's fast enough by default: you describe the whole screen for the current state, and React batches and minimises the DOM writes, so you don't need to hand-optimise every transition to avoid layout thrashing.

That's why frameworks like Svelte and Solid skip the virtual DOM entirely and compile to direct updates, and why React's own direction — the compiler — is about doing less render work, not a faster diff."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: raw speed vs a fast-enough declarative model
stages.html: "The virtual DOM is overhead paid for a programming model, not a performance feature."

stages.name: Where direct DOM wins
stages.html:
• One text node change: direct write is one operation; React re-runs the component, diffs, then writes.
  • High-frequency updates (60 fps canvas-like visuals, token streams into a huge list) can need direct DOM or refs.

stages.name: Where React's model wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the work per update (conceptual):

Direct:  compute change → 1 DOM write
React:   call component(s) → build elements → diff → same DOM write(s)
         + automatic batching of many state changes into one commit
  • Across a large app, batching and avoiding stale DOM state usually matter more than per-update overhead.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: is the bottleneck render work or DOM work?
stages.html: • Profile: if component render time dominates, reduce renders (state placement, memo, compiler); if DOM work dominates, reduce DOM (virtualisation).

stages.name: What I'd say
stages.html: • React for app UIs; escape hatches (refs, direct DOM, canvas) for hot paths like streaming visualisations.

followUps.question: 🧪 A component re-renders but produces an identical element tree. How many DOM writes happen?
followUps.html: Zero: the diff finds nothing to change. The cost paid was the render and diff, which is why unnecessary re-renders still cost CPU even without DOM writes.

followUps.question: "Virtual DOM is why React is fast."
followUps.html: It's why React is fast enough while declarative. Direct DOM or compiled frameworks can be faster.

followUps.question: How do Svelte and Solid avoid it?
followUps.html: They compile components into code that updates exactly the DOM nodes affected by each piece of state (fine-grained reactivity), so no tree diff is needed.

followUps.question: Where does React spend time in practice?
followUps.html: Mostly in running component functions and their work (and effects), not in the diff. The Profiler's render timings show it.

followUps.question: Would you drop to direct DOM in a React app?
followUps.html: For hot paths only — a streaming token display, a chart, a canvas — isolated in one component with a ref, keeping React for the rest. Measure first.

react-q7.testing: hooks are matched by call order, not by name.
react-q7.trap: reciting "the rules of hooks say so".
react-q7.spoken:
"Because React identifies hooks by the order they're called, not by name. Each component instance has a fiber, and on the fiber there's a linked list of hook states. On every render, the first useState call reads the first node, the second call reads the second node, and so on. Nothing in useState('') says which piece of state it is; its position is its identity.

If a condition skips a hook on one render, every hook after it reads the wrong node: the third hook gets the second hook's state, possibly a different kind of hook altogether. React catches some of these — if some hooks ran and then fewer or more ran than last time, it throws 'rendered fewer hooks than expected' — but not all, so the rule is enforced statically by the ESLint plugin.

The fix is to call hooks unconditionally at the top and put the condition inside the hook or the render output, or split the conditional part into its own component, which gets its own hook list. The exception is use in React 19: it isn't slot-based, so it can be called conditionally (Q38)."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "Hook state is stored in call order; skipping a call shifts every later hook onto someone else's state."

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
render 1: useState('a') → node 0 · useEffect → node 1 · useState(0) → node 2
render 2 (condition skips the first): useEffect reads node 0 (a state node!) · useState(0) reads node 1

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: React's runtime check fires when the count changes after some hooks ran
stages.html:
function P({ userId }) {
  const [x] = useState(0)
  if (!userId) return <p>login</p>
  const [n] = useState('')
  return <input value={n} readOnly />
}
// render userId="42", then userId={null}
// → throws "Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement."
// render null, then "42"
// → throws "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render."   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.claim: early returns, loops, silent state loss
stages.html:
• Early returns before hooks (Q33), hooks in loops with changing length, hooks inside conditions or callbacks.
  • Some violations don't throw (e.g. zero hooks before an early return) and silently lose state — which is why the lint rule, not the runtime, is the real guard.

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html: • 19: use(promise | context) may be conditional; all other hooks keep the ordering rule. The React Compiler also assumes the rules of hooks hold.

followUps.question: items.map(item => useState(item)) in a component — safe?
followUps.html: Only while items.length never changes. The moment it does, the hook count changes and React throws or misassigns state. Move per-item state into a child component per item.

followUps.question: "Hooks can't be conditional because React said so."
followUps.html: The reason is mechanical: order is identity. Knowing that lets you predict which patterns are safe (a hook inside a child component) and which aren't.

followUps.question: Why didn't React use keys or names for hooks?
followUps.html: Order keeps the API tiny (useState(init)), composes through custom hooks automatically, and avoids name collisions between hooks from different libraries. The cost is this rule.

followUps.question: How do custom hooks fit?
followUps.html: A custom hook is just a function calling hooks; its hooks occupy consecutive slots in the caller's list, so the same ordering rule applies to calling it.

followUps.question: How do you enforce this across a team?
followUps.html: eslint-plugin-react-hooks (rules-of-hooks as error) in CI, plus the compiler's own lint when adopting the React Compiler.

dontSay: "React will always throw if you break it."
Hooks inside loops over variable-length arrays.

react-q8.testing: stale closures in effects, and fixing them without lying to the dependency array.
react-q8.trap: "just add count to the dependency array" without seeing the cost.
react-q8.spoken:
"B: the interval callback closed over count from the first render.

The effect runs once, because of the empty dependency array, and creates an interval whose callback captured count = 0. Every tick it calls setCount(0 + 1). The first tick changes 0 to 1; every later tick sets 1 again, which React ignores. So it shows 1 and stops.

The fix is the updater form: setCount(c => c + 1). Then the effect doesn't read count at all, the empty array is honest, and one interval runs for the component's lifetime.

Adding count to the dependencies also works, but it tears down and recreates the interval every second, which drifts the timing."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Timer() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const id = setInterval(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000);
    return () => clearInterval(id);
  }, []);
  return <h1>{count}</h1>;
}
  • A: clearInterval runs too early · B: the interval closes over count from the first render · C: setCount is not batched inside setInterval · D: the empty dep array is illegal here

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Tick count in closure Update Screen
1 0 set 1 1
2 0 set 1 (bail out) 1
3… 0 set 1 1

Prove it:

// interval shortened to 20 ms, read after ~130 ms
// → "1"                        (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
// with setCount(c => c + 1)
// → keeps counting

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: effects see the render they were created in
stages.html: • The effect's closure is a snapshot of that render's props and state. An empty dependency array means "never re-sync", so the snapshot never updates.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Behaviour
setCount(c => c + 1), deps [] counts correctly, one interval
setCount(count + 1), deps [count] counts, but interval recreated every tick
reading latest value via a ref works; use for non-state values (callbacks, props)
useEffectEvent (React 19.2+) non-reactive latest-value callback inside effects

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Polling that sends stale filters, websocket handlers using old props: same bug. Use updaters for state, refs or useEffectEvent for latest props, and honest dependency arrays.

followUps.question: Change the callback to setCount(c => c + 1) and keep []. What does StrictMode dev show on mount?
followUps.html: It counts normally. StrictMode mounts, runs cleanup (clearing the first interval), and mounts again, so exactly one interval survives.

followUps.question: "Disable the exhaustive-deps lint rule."
followUps.html: That hides the stale closure instead of fixing it. Remove the dependency by using an updater or useEffectEvent, don't lie about it.

followUps.question: Why is [count] a worse fix?
followUps.html: Each change clears and recreates the interval, so ticks restart their timer and drift; it also churns effects on every update.

followUps.question: What is useEffectEvent?
followUps.html: A hook for logic called from effects that should see the latest props/state without making the effect re-run — for example logging with the current user inside a connection effect.

followUps.question: Where have you seen this in production?
followUps.html: A live dashboard poller kept requesting data for the filters selected at mount time. The fix was keying the polling effect on the filters (re-subscribe on change) and using the updater for local counters.

react-q9.testing: dependency arrays compare by reference, and the fix belongs where the object is created.
react-q9.spoken:
"React compares dependencies with Object.is, which for objects means reference equality. If filters is an object literal created during render — in this component or in a parent that passes it down — it's a new object every render, so the dependency 'changed' every time, even when the values are identical, and the effect re-runs. If the effect fetches data and sets state, that's also a loop or a flood of requests.

I'd confirm by logging whether prevFilters === filters or checking where the object is created.

The fix belongs at the creation site. Depend on the primitive values the effect actually uses — filters.status, filters.page — or memoize the object with useMemo where it's created, or keep filters in state or the URL so the reference only changes when the user changes them. What I don't do is delete it from the array, which hides a stale-closure bug."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.claim: runs every render, often a request flood
stages.html: • Network tab: the same request repeatedly; sometimes a render loop if the effect sets state.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
Prove it — an inline object vs a memoized one:

function Search({ q }) { const filters = { q }; useEffect(() => { runs++ }, [filters]); return null }
// 4 renders with the same q
// → effect runs: 4
function Search2({ q }) { const filters = useMemo(() => ({ q }), [q]); useEffect(() => { runs2++ }, [filters]); return null }
// → effect runs: 1        (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Where
object/array literal in render this component
object built in a parent and passed as a prop parent
derived arrays (items.filter(...)) this component
functions defined in render used as deps this component (useCallback or move inside effect)

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html: • why-did-you-render or a quick useRef comparison of the previous value; React DevTools shows which props changed.

stages.name: Fix
stages.html:
Fix When
depend on primitives ([filters.q, filters.page]) effect uses a few fields
useMemo where the object is built object needed as a whole
keep filters in state / URL user-controlled filters
move the object inside the effect only the effect uses it
a query library keyed by filters data fetching (dedupes and caches)

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.html: • exhaustive-deps lint on; review rule "no object literals as dependencies"; the React Compiler memoizes such objects automatically where it can.

followUps.question: useEffect(fn, [ [a, b] ]) — how often does it run?
followUps.html: Every render: [a, b] is a new array each time. Use [a, b] as the dependency list itself, not an array inside it.

followUps.question: "Remove filters from the array."
followUps.html: The effect then uses stale filters forever — a silent bug instead of a noisy one.

followUps.question: Why doesn't React deep-compare dependencies?
followUps.html: Deep comparison costs time on every render and can be wrong for mutable objects; reference equality is cheap and predictable.

followUps.question: What if filters comes from a parent I can't change?
followUps.html: Depend on its primitive fields, or derive a stable key (e.g. JSON.stringify for small, serialisable objects) — acceptable in small doses.

followUps.question: The effect fetches data. What's the architectural fix?
followUps.html: Move server data to a query library keyed by the filter values; it dedupes identical keys, caches, and cancels stale requests, so effect-based fetching disappears (Q25).

react-q10.testing: automatic batching in React 18, and where batching used to stop.
react-q10.spoken:
"B: two in React 17, one in React 18 and later.

In React 17, updates were only batched inside React's own event handlers. Here the updates happen inside a setTimeout callback — after the click handler has returned — so React 17 processed each setState separately: two re-renders.

React 18 introduced automatic batching with createRoot: updates are batched wherever they happen — timeouts, promises, native event listeners — so the two updates produce one re-render.

If I ever need an update applied immediately, for example to measure the DOM before the next update, flushSync is the opt-out."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [a, setA] = useState(0);
  const [b, setB] = useState(0);
  const handleClick = () => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      setA(x => x + 1);
      setB(x => x + 1);
    }, 0);
  };
  return <button onClick={handleClick}>{a}{b}</button>;
}
  • A: 1 then 1 · B: 2 then 1 · C: 1 then 2 · D: 2 then 2

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
React 17 React 18+
inside the click handler batched batched
inside setTimeout / promise not batched → 2 renders batched → 1 render

Prove it:

// count renders after one click, once the timeout fires
// → re-renders: 1, button shows "11"     (React 19.3, createRoot, jsdom harness)

React 17's two renders come from its documented behaviour; not re-measured here.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html: • 17: batching tied to React's event system. 18+: batching tied to the scheduler, for any update within the same task, when using createRoot. Legacy ReactDOM.render keeps old behaviour.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: flushSync and legacy roots opt out
stages.html:
Variant Renders (18+)
wrap setA in flushSync 2
updates in two separate timeouts 2
legacy ReactDOM.render root (18) 2

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Upgrading to 18 usually reduces renders; code that read DOM right after a setState in a timeout (expecting it applied) may break — that's where flushSync appears.

followUps.question: In React 18, await fetch(...) in a handler, then setA(1); setB(1). How many renders?
followUps.html: One: updates after an await in the same task are batched automatically.

followUps.question: "React always batched updates."
followUps.html: Only inside React event handlers before 18. Timeouts, promises and native listeners caused a render per update.

followUps.question: When would you use flushSync?
followUps.html: When you must read layout after a state change synchronously — e.g. scroll to a newly added item — or integrate with a non-React library expecting the DOM updated. Rare, and it costs performance.

followUps.question: Does batching change the final state?
followUps.html: No, only the number of renders and when you can observe intermediate states. Updaters still apply in order.

followUps.question: What would you check when upgrading a large app from 17?
followUps.html: Code reading DOM or refs right after setState outside handlers, tests asserting intermediate renders, and third-party libraries relying on synchronous updates — plus the StrictMode double-effect behaviour (Q12).

dontSay: "Batching is only for event handlers" (true only before 18).

react-q11.testing: timing relative to paint, the flicker case, and the cost.
react-q11.trap: "useLayoutEffect is the synchronous, more correct one — use it for safety."
react-q11.spoken:
"The difference is timing relative to paint. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after React commits DOM changes but before the browser paints. useEffect runs after paint.

That makes useLayoutEffect the tool for one job: measure the DOM and correct it before the user sees the frame. The real case I've needed it for is positioning a tooltip or popover: I render it, measure its size and the anchor's position, and if it would overflow the viewport, flip it above. Doing that in useEffect shows the wrong position for one frame — a visible flicker. Scroll restoration and syncing a third-party DOM widget are similar.

The cost is that it blocks painting, so heavy work there makes the UI feel slow, and it doesn't run on the server — during SSR it warns and does nothing. So useEffect is the default for everything else: data fetching, subscriptions, logging, analytics."

stages.name: Frame the axis
Where useEffect wins
stages.html: • Fetching, subscriptions, timers, analytics, syncing to storage: doesn't need to block the frame.

stages.name: Where useLayoutEffect wins
stages.html:
Prove it — the tooltip pattern:

function Tooltip({ anchorRect, children }) {
  const ref = useRef(null)
  const [top, setTop] = useState(anchorRect.bottom)
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    const h = ref.current.getBoundingClientRect().height
    if (anchorRect.bottom + h > window.innerHeight) setTop(anchorRect.top - h)   // flip above
  }, [anchorRect])
  return <div ref={ref} style={{ position: 'fixed', top }}>{children}</div>
}
// with useEffect: one painted frame at the wrong position (flicker); with useLayoutEffect: none

The re-render triggered inside useLayoutEffect is committed before paint, so the user only sees the corrected position.

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: would the user see a wrong frame?
stages.html: • Yes → layout effect (keep it tiny). No → useEffect.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: useEffect by default, layout effect by exception
stages.html: • Popovers, measuring text to truncate, scroll restoration: layout. Everything else: effect. SSR components: guard layout work or use useEffect with a hidden-until-measured style.

followUps.question: In a layout effect you call setState. When does the user see it?
followUps.html: In the same paint: React processes that update synchronously before the browser paints, so no intermediate frame appears.

followUps.question: "useLayoutEffect is safer because it's synchronous."
followUps.html: It's more blocking, not safer. Using it by default delays paint and hurts responsiveness.

followUps.question: What happens during SSR?
followUps.html: Layout effects don't run on the server; React warns about the mismatch between server output and client behaviour. Use useEffect or render measurement-dependent UI only on the client.

followUps.question: Where does useInsertionEffect fit?
followUps.html: It runs before layout effects, for CSS-in-JS libraries to inject styles before anything reads layout. Application code rarely needs it.

followUps.question: INP got worse after a refactor. You find a layout effect doing heavy work. What now?
followUps.html: Move non-layout work to useEffect, keep only the measurement in the layout effect, and cache measurements. Verify with the Performance panel that the long task is gone.

react-q12.testing: StrictMode's mount–unmount–mount simulation and why cleanup must be correct.
react-q12.trap: adding a useRef guard to "fix" the double effect.
react-q12.spoken:
"C: effect, cleanup, effect.

In development, StrictMode deliberately mounts the component, runs its effects, then simulates an unmount — running the cleanups — and mounts again, running the effects a second time. It only happens in development.

It's simulating something real: React may unmount and remount components while preserving their state — for example with the Activity API, fast refresh, or future features that keep UI alive offscreen. An effect that isn't cleaned up properly — a subscription never unsubscribed, a connection never closed, a timer never cleared — leaks or duplicates when that happens. StrictMode surfaces the bug now.

So the fix for a 'double' effect is a correct cleanup, never a ref that stops the effect from running twice."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Child() {
  useEffect(() => {
    console.log('effect');
    return () => console.log('cleanup');
  }, []);
  return null;
}
  • A: effect · B: effect, effect · C: effect, cleanup, effect · D: effect, cleanup

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// <StrictMode><Child /></StrictMode>, development build
// → effect, cleanup, effect     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
// production build or no StrictMode
// → effect

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html: • Effect + cleanup should be symmetrical: mounting twice with a cleanup in between must behave like mounting once.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Behaviour
no cleanup, subscription in effect two subscriptions in dev — the bug StrictMode reveals
fetch without cleanup two requests; harmless if idempotent, but results can race (Q13)
useRef "ran once" guard hides the bug; breaks under real remounts

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Chat sockets, event listeners, intervals: correct cleanup prevents duplicate messages and memory leaks when components remount for real.

followUps.question: An effect does ws = new WebSocket(url) with no cleanup. What happens in dev StrictMode?
followUps.html: Two sockets open; both deliver messages, so handlers fire twice. Add return () => ws.close().

followUps.question: "Add a ref so the effect only runs once."
followUps.html: That suppresses the warning signal and leaves the leak for real remounts. Fix the cleanup.

followUps.question: Does StrictMode also double-render?
followUps.html: Yes, in development it calls component functions twice to surface impure render logic, so logs in render can appear twice (React DevTools can dim the duplicate).

followUps.question: Should analytics "page view" effects fire twice?
followUps.html: In dev only; in production they fire once. If double counting in dev is annoying, filter dev events rather than guarding the effect.

followUps.question: Your team disabled StrictMode because of double fetches. Your call?
followUps.html: Re-enable it, and move data fetching to a query library or framework loader that dedupes and caches; fix cleanups. The double fetch is a symptom of effect-based fetching.

dontSay: A ref guard as the fix.

react-q13.testing: out-of-order responses, and using effect cleanup to invalidate a request.
react-q13.trap: debouncing as the fix — it reduces the chance, not the bug.
react-q13.spoken:
"It's a race: two requests are in flight, responses can arrive in any order, and the code sets state with whichever arrives last. Typing 'a' then 'ab' fires two fetches; if 'a' is slower, its results land after 'ab' and overwrite them, so the screen shows results for a query that's no longer in the box.

The fix is to make each effect run invalidate its own request when it's superseded. In the effect, I set a local ignore = false; the cleanup, which runs before the next effect when the query changes, sets ignore = true; and the .then only sets state if ignore is still false. Better still, pass an AbortController signal to fetch and abort in the cleanup, which also cancels the network request.

Debouncing helps load but doesn't fix correctness, because two requests can still overlap.

At scale I don't hand-roll this: a query library like TanStack Query keys requests by the query value, so only the current key's data is shown, and it handles caching and cancellation."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html: • Intermittent, worse on slow networks; results for an earlier query appear after typing more.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html: • Throttle the network in DevTools or add artificial latency so the older request is slower; watch the response order.

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Tell
no cancellation/ignore in the effect last-arriving response wins
shared state updated from several sources overwrites from other components
caching layer returning stale key wrong data for current key

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it — 'a' takes 60 ms, 'ab' takes 10 ms:

function Results({ query, guard }) {
  const [data, setData] = useState('')
  useEffect(() => {
    let ignore = false
    delay(query === 'a' ? 60 : 10, 'results for ' + query).then(d => { if (!guard || !ignore) setData(d) })
    return () => { ignore = true }
  }, [query])
  return <p>{data}</p>
}
// render query="a", then "ab"; wait 100 ms
// → guard=false  "results for a"    (stale wins)
// → guard=true   "results for ab"   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Fix
stages.claim: invalidate in cleanup, or let a library key it
stages.html:
useEffect(() => {
  const ctrl = new AbortController()
  fetch(`/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
    .then(r => r.json()).then(setResults)
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setError(e) })
  return () => ctrl.abort()
}, [query])
  • Or useQuery({ queryKey: ['search', query], queryFn }).

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.html: • A test with a mocked slow first response (MSW with delays) asserting the latest results win; a lint/review rule that data-fetching effects must clean up.

followUps.question: With the ignore flag but no abort, how many network requests complete when typing 'a','b','c' quickly?
followUps.html: All three complete on the network; only the last one's result is applied. AbortController also cancels the earlier requests, saving bandwidth and server work.

followUps.question: "Debounce the input — fixed."
followUps.html: Debouncing reduces the number of requests; any two that still overlap can arrive out of order. You still need invalidation.

followUps.question: Why does the cleanup run at the right time?
followUps.html: When query changes, React runs the previous effect's cleanup before running the new effect, so the old request is marked stale exactly when it's superseded — and on unmount.

followUps.question: Where does useTransition fit?
followUps.html: It keeps the old results visible while new ones render, improving perceived responsiveness; it doesn't solve the network race by itself.

followUps.question: Same problem in a streaming AI chat: user sends a second message while the first is streaming. Design?
followUps.html: Give each run an ID; abort the previous stream (AbortController on the fetch/SSE) or let it finish into its own message; only append tokens for the active run ID; server-side, cancel the upstream generation to stop paying for tokens.

D4 Large Lists and Noisy Input

react-q14.testing: the argument is evaluated by JavaScript every render; lazy initialisers fix it.
react-q14.trap: answering 1 because "useState only uses the initial value once".
react-q14.spoken:
"B: five times.

useState(buildGrid()) is ordinary JavaScript: the argument is evaluated before useState is even called, on every render. React uses the value only on the first render and ignores it afterwards, but the work has already been done.

The fix is lazy initialisation: pass the function, useState(buildGrid) or useState(() => buildGrid(size)). React calls it once, on mount, and never again."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [grid, setGrid] = useState(buildGrid());
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>;
}
  • A: 1 · B: 5 · C: 0 · D: 2

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.claim: the call happens before useState sees it
stages.html:
Prove it:

// mount + 4 clicks = 5 renders
// → buildGrid called 5 times              (React 19.3, jsdom harness, no StrictMode)
// with useState(buildGrid)
// → 1

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html: • JavaScript evaluates f(g()) by calling g first. React can only discard the value, not prevent the call.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Calls over 5 renders
useState(buildGrid) 1
useState(() => buildGrid(10)) 1
StrictMode dev, lazy initialiser 2 on mount (double render), then none
useMemo(() => buildGrid(), []) 1 (but memo is a cache hint, not a guarantee)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • useState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('draft'))) in an input component parses storage on every keystroke; lazy initialisers fix it.

followUps.question: useState(() => buildGrid()) in StrictMode development — how many calls on mount?
followUps.html: Two: StrictMode double-invokes render (and initialisers) in development to surface impurity. Production: one.

followUps.question: "React only runs the initial value once."
followUps.html: React only uses it once; JavaScript evaluates it every render.

followUps.question: Why not useMemo for this?
followUps.html: Memo is a performance hint React may discard (e.g. offscreen); lazy state is guaranteed to initialise once and becomes real state you can update.

followUps.question: Does useReducer have the same issue?
followUps.html: Yes; its third argument init gives lazy initialisation: useReducer(reducer, arg, init).

followUps.question: Where would you spot this in a code review?
followUps.html: Any useState(someCall(...)) where the call reads storage, parses, or builds large structures — suggest the lazy form; the profiler shows it as repeated work per render.

react-q15.spoken:
"B: child effect, then parent effect.

Rendering goes top-down — the parent renders first and produces the child — but effects run after the commit, bottom-up: children's effects before their parent's. That's deliberate: when a parent's effect runs, it can rely on all its descendants' DOM nodes, refs and effects already being set up — for example, measuring or focusing a child element."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Parent() {
  useEffect(() => console.log('parent effect'), []);
  return <Child />;
}
function Child() {
  useEffect(() => console.log('child effect'), []);
  return null;
}
  • A: parent effect, child effect · B: child effect, parent effect · C: order is not guaranteed · D: only parent effect

stages.name: Trace the commit
stages.html:
Prove it:

// → child effect, parent effect     (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
Phase Order
render Parent → Child
commit DOM Child's DOM inside Parent's
effects (layout and passive) Child → Parent
cleanups on unmount Parent → Child

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: a parent's effect sees a finished subtree
stages.html: • React completes work bottom-up; effects fire in completion order, so children are ready before parents.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: layout effects run before passive ones
stages.html:
Variant Order
both useLayoutEffect child, parent
parent useLayoutEffect, child useEffect parent (layout, before paint), then child (passive)
siblings in tree order, each subtree bottom-up

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • A dialog's effect can focus its first input because the input's DOM exists; a child effect that depends on the parent's effect having run first is fragile — pass data down instead.

followUps.question: Parent uses useLayoutEffect, child uses useEffect. Order?
followUps.html: parent layout first (layout effects run during commit, before paint), then child effect (passive effects after paint).

followUps.question: "Parent effects run first because the parent renders first."
followUps.html: Rendering and effects have different orders: render is top-down, effects bottom-up.

followUps.question: Why would React design it that way?
followUps.html: So a parent can safely use its children's DOM and refs in its effect: they're guaranteed to exist.

followUps.question: What order do cleanups run on unmount?
followUps.html: Parent before child — the reverse of setup — so parents tear down before their children disappear.

followUps.question: A child fetches data in an effect and the parent also fetches. What's the problem?
followUps.html: A waterfall: the child's fetch starts only after the parent's render tree mounts, and if the parent gates rendering on its data, requests serialise. Hoist fetching to route loaders or start requests in parallel (Server Components, query prefetching).

dontSay: Relying on a child effect running after the parent's.
