react-q16.testing: refs as a mutable box React doesn't watch, and choosing ref vs state.
react-q16.spoken:
"A ref is a plain mutable object, { current }, that React keeps stable for the component's lifetime. React doesn't track writes to it — there's no setter, no scheduling — so changing ref.current never triggers a render. State, by contrast, goes through setState, which schedules a render.

That's exactly what you want for values the screen doesn't display: a DOM node handle, a timer or interval ID, an AbortController, the previous value of a prop, the latest callback for a subscription, or a counter you only read inside handlers.

It's a bug the moment the value belongs on screen: the UI shows whatever was current at the last render, and it silently goes stale. Also, don't read or write refs during render, because it makes render impure — do it in effects and handlers."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: a mutable box React doesn't watch
stages.html: "State is watched and triggers renders; a ref is stable storage that doesn't."

stages.name: What React does
stages.html:
useState useRef
change triggers render yes no
value per render snapshot always latest
use for displayed data handles, IDs, latest values for callbacks

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
function RefBox() {
  renders++
  const ref = useRef(0)
  bump = () => { ref.current++ }
  return <p>{ref.current}</p>
}
// call bump() three times
// → renders: 1, shown: "0"          (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html: • Displayed values in refs go stale; reading ref.current in render; mutating refs during render (breaks concurrent rendering assumptions).

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html: • 19: ref is a regular prop for function components (no forwardRef needed); ref callbacks can return a cleanup function.

followUps.question: After bump() ×3, the parent re-renders for another reason. What's shown?
followUps.html: "3": the next render reads the latest ref.current. The value was never lost, just not displayed until something else rendered — the classic stale-UI bug.

followUps.question: "Use refs to avoid re-renders for performance."
followUps.html: Only for values not shown on screen. Using refs for displayed data trades a render for a wrong UI.

followUps.question: How do you keep the latest callback for a subscription?
followUps.html: Store it in a ref updated in an effect (or use useEffectEvent), and have the long-lived subscription call ref.current().

followUps.question: How do you track a previous prop value?
followUps.html: Store it in a ref and update it in an effect; or better, store the previous value in state and compare during render (React docs pattern) when it affects output.

followUps.question: In a streaming chat, where do refs help?
followUps.html: Holding the AbortController for the active stream, a buffer of incoming tokens flushed to state on requestAnimationFrame, and the scroll container for auto-scroll — none of which should re-render on every token.

dontSay: Reading refs in render for display.

links.label: H4 Refs and Imperative Escape Hatches

react-q17.testing: shallow prop comparison and reference identity of inline objects and functions.
react-q17.trap: "memo is broken" or "memo does a deep compare".
react-q17.spoken:
"React.memo skips a re-render only if every prop is equal by Object.is to last time — a shallow compare. The parent passes style={{ color: 'red' }} and onSelect={() => …}, both created fresh during each render. They look identical but they're new references, so the comparison fails every time and Child re-renders; the memo is pure overhead.

To make memo work, the props must be stable: hoist the constant style object outside the component, and wrap the handler in useCallback, or pass a stable function. Or, often better, ask whether the memo is needed at all — and with the React Compiler enabled, these inline values are memoized automatically."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
const Child = React.memo(({ style, onSelect }) => {
  console.log('child render');
  return <div style={style} onClick={onSelect} />;
});
function Parent() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return (
    <>
      <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>{n}</button>
      <Child style={{ color: 'red' }} onSelect={() => console.log('pick')} />
    </>
  );
}

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// mount + 2 clicks = 3 parent renders
// → child renders: 3                    (React 19.3, jsdom harness)
Prop Render 1 Render 2 Object.is
style {color:'red'} #1 {color:'red'} #2 false
onSelect fn #1 fn #2 false

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html: • memo compares each prop with Object.is; objects, arrays and functions compare by reference.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Change Child renders over 3 parent renders
const RED = { color: 'red' } outside + useCallback handler 1
only style hoisted, handler still inline 3
React Compiler enabled 1 (auto-memoized)
children prop as JSX 3 (JSX elements are new objects)

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Profiler shows memoized components rendering with "props changed: style, onSelect". Fix the sources or drop the memo.

followUps.question: You hoist style but pass onSelect={handleSelect} where handleSelect is a plain function inside Parent. Renders?
followUps.html: Still every time: handleSelect is recreated each render. Wrap it in useCallback (with correct deps) or move it outside if it doesn't use props/state.

followUps.question: "memo deep-compares props."
followUps.html: It's shallow. You can pass a custom comparator as the second argument, but deep comparisons are costly and error-prone.

followUps.question: Why does passing children break memo?
followUps.html: <Child><Icon /></Child> creates a new element object for children every parent render, so the prop changes by reference.

followUps.question: Is the failed memo harmful?
followUps.html: Slightly: React does the comparison and then renders anyway — cost with no benefit, plus code noise.

followUps.question: How would you fix a slow list whose rows are memoized but still re-render?
followUps.html: Profile to see which props change; stabilise them at the source (ids instead of objects, useCallback for handlers, pass primitives), or adopt the React Compiler; if rows are many, virtualise first (Q31).

react-q18.testing: memoization as a measured tool, and cheaper structural fixes first.
react-q18.trap: "memo everything to be safe" or "memo is always bad".
react-q18.spoken:
"I'd ask for the profile that motivated it. Memoization is a cache: it costs memory, a comparison on every render, dependency arrays that must stay correct, and noise that hides the real logic. It only pays off when a component is expensive to render and its props are actually stable — and blanket useCallback often doesn't achieve that, because one inline object further up breaks the chain.

Before memo, I'd try structural fixes that make re-renders cheap or unnecessary: move state down closer to where it's used, so fewer components re-render; lift expensive subtrees out by passing them as children, so they aren't re-created when the stateful parent changes; and split contexts so consumers don't all re-render.

Then memo where the profiler shows a real hot spot, with stable props.

And if the team is on React 19 with the React Compiler, most manual memoization becomes redundant — the compiler memoizes automatically where it can prove it's safe — so I'd rather invest in keeping components pure than in hand-written useCallback."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: skipped work vs cost and complexity
stages.html: "Memoization trades comparison cost and maintenance for skipped render work; it's worth it only where that work is big and props are stable."

stages.name: Where memoization wins
stages.html: • Large lists or charts whose inputs rarely change; values passed to memoized children or used as effect dependencies.

stages.name: Where it costs
stages.html:
Cost Detail
comparison per render props or deps checked every time
stale-deps bugs wrong dependency arrays → stale values
broken chains one unstable prop defeats the whole memo
readability intent buried under wrappers

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: did the profiler show this component as a cost?
stages.html:
Prove it — the cheaper structural fix (children pattern):

function Page() {
  return <ScrollTracker><ExpensiveTree /></ScrollTracker>   // ExpensiveTree created by Page
}
function ScrollTracker({ children }) {
  const [y, setY] = useState(0)                            // updates often
  useEffect(() => { const f = () => setY(scrollY); addEventListener('scroll', f); return () => removeEventListener('scroll', f) }, [])
  return <div data-y={y}>{children}</div>                  // children element is the same object → not re-rendered
}

ScrollTracker re-renders on every scroll; ExpensiveTree doesn't, with no memo at all, because its element was created by Page, which didn't re-render.

stages.name: What I'd say in review
stages.html: • "Please remove memo/useCallback where the profiler shows no cost; keep it on X and Y where it measurably helps; consider moving state down here; with the compiler we'll drop most of these."

followUps.question: A memoized component receives items={data.filter(x => x.active)} from its parent. Does memo help?
followUps.html: No: filter returns a new array every render. Memoize the filtered array with useMemo in the parent, or pass data and filter inside the child.

followUps.question: "Memoization is free, so wrap everything."
followUps.html: It costs comparisons, memory and correctness risk; unmeasured, it often buys nothing.

followUps.question: What does the React Compiler change?
followUps.html: It auto-memoizes components and values it can prove are pure, so hand-written memo/useCallback become mostly unnecessary where it applies (Q40).

followUps.question: Why does moving state down help?
followUps.html: Only the component owning the state and its subtree re-render; siblings and the rest of the page don't.

followUps.question: How do you make this a team standard?
followUps.html: A short guideline ("profile first; prefer structure; memo only proven hot spots"), a performance check in the PR template, and adoption of the compiler with its lint rules rather than manual memo rules.

dontSay: A review comment without asking for a profile.

react-q19.trap: inventing a difference ("useCallback prevents re-creating the function").
react-q19.spoken:
"Nothing. useCallback(fn, deps) is exactly useMemo(() => fn, deps). Both return the same value across renders until a dependency changes; useCallback is just the convenient spelling when the value you want to keep stable is a function.

One common misconception: useCallback doesn't stop the function from being created. The inline function is still created every render; useCallback returns the previous one instead. The point is a stable reference — for a memoized child, or an effect's dependency — not skipping work. useMemo is the one used to skip an expensive computation."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html: "useCallback(fn, deps) ≡ useMemo(() => fn, deps)."

stages.name: Trace the equivalence
stages.html:
Prove it:

function Same({ n }) {
  const a = useCallback(() => n, [n])
  const b = useMemo(() => () => n, [n])
  pair.push([a, b])
  return null
}
// render twice with n = 1; compare render 1 vs render 2
// → stable across renders: true true        (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: both cache a value by deps
stages.html:
returns purpose
useMemo(calc, deps) calc() result skip recomputation / stable object
useCallback(fn, deps) fn itself stable function reference

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
• Missing a dependency → both return a stale function/value.
  • React Compiler enabled → both mostly unnecessary.

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Callbacks passed to memoized children, used in effect deps, or passed to custom hooks that depend on identity.

followUps.question: const onSave = useCallback(() => save(form), []). What does it save after the user edits the form?
followUps.html: The original form from the first render: the empty dependency list froze a stale closure. Add form to the deps (or read it from a ref/updater).

followUps.question: "useCallback prevents creating a new function each render."
followUps.html: The function literal is still created; useCallback just returns the cached one.

followUps.question: When is useCallback pointless?
followUps.html: When the function goes to a non-memoized child or a DOM element: nothing compares its identity.

followUps.question: Is useMemo a guarantee?
followUps.html: No, it's a performance hint; React may discard cached values. Don't rely on it for correctness.

followUps.question: How does the compiler change your reviews here?
followUps.html: With the compiler, manual useCallback/useMemo rarely matters; reviews focus on purity and correct deps where manual memo remains.

react-q20.testing: single source of truth, subscribing to history, push vs replace, serialisation.
react-q20.trap: keeping a useState copy synced to the URL with effects.
react-q20.spoken:
"I'd mirror useState: const [page, setPage] = useQueryParam('page', { parse, serialize, default, history: 'replace' }), so it drops into existing code.

The key decision is that the URL is the single source of truth. The hook doesn't keep its own state and sync it with effects — that creates two sources of truth that drift, especially with back and forward. Instead it reads the current value from the location and subscribes to changes. The right primitive for subscribing to an external source is useSyncExternalStore, subscribing to popstate plus my own navigation events, with a server snapshot for SSR.

The hard parts: serialisation — numbers, booleans, arrays, dates — with safe parsing of hand-edited URLs and a default for invalid values; push versus replace — a filter change might be replace, a page change a push, so it's an explicit option; batching several params in one navigation so the URL doesn't churn; debouncing text inputs so each keystroke doesn't create history entries; and SSR consistency, so the server and client read the same value.

In Next.js, I'd build on useSearchParams and router.replace, since the router owns the URL."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.claim: which state belongs in the URL?
stages.html: • Shareable, bookmarkable, back-button-meaningful state: filters, tabs, pagination, search. Not ephemeral UI (hover, open menus).

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • Back/forward must work; SSR must match; typing shouldn't flood history; invalid URLs must not crash.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: URL as source, subscribe to it
stages.html:
Prove it — the core, framework-agnostic:

function subscribe(cb) { addEventListener('popstate', cb); addEventListener('urlchange', cb); return () => { removeEventListener('popstate', cb); removeEventListener('urlchange', cb) } }
function useQueryParam(key, { parse = String, serialize = String, fallback, history: mode = 'replace' } = {}) {
  const raw = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, () => new URLSearchParams(location.search).get(key), () => null)
  const value = raw == null ? fallback : parse(raw)
  const setValue = useCallback(next => {
    const p = new URLSearchParams(location.search); p.set(key, serialize(next))
    window.history[mode === 'push' ? 'pushState' : 'replaceState'](null, '', `?${p}`)
    dispatchEvent(new Event('urlchange'))
  }, [key, serialize, mode])
  return [value, setValue]
}

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Hard part Approach
typed values parse/serialize per param; schema validation (zod) with fallback
push vs replace explicit option; filters replace, navigation push
several params at once a setParams({...}) batch API
typing debounce URL writes; keep input value local while typing
SSR server snapshot from request params; same parse on both sides

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Two sources of truth drifting (state + URL); history spam; crashes on ?page=abc; hydration mismatch when the server ignores params.

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html: • Next.js: useSearchParams, usePathname, router.replace(url, { scroll: false }); libraries like nuqs implement this pattern with types.

followUps.question: A search box writes every keystroke to the URL with pushState. User types "react" then presses Back. What happens?
followUps.html: The URL goes to "reac" — one history entry per keystroke. Use replace (or debounce and push once) for typing.

followUps.question: "useState + useEffect to sync with the URL is fine."
followUps.html: It creates two sources of truth; back/forward, external navigation and concurrent renders make them drift. Read from the URL directly.

followUps.question: Why useSyncExternalStore here?
followUps.html: The URL is an external mutable source; this hook subscribes correctly and prevents tearing during concurrent rendering (Q21).

followUps.question: How do you test it?
followUps.html: RTL with a memory history: set URL → assert value; call setter → assert URL and history length; simulate popstate → assert re-render; invalid param → fallback.

followUps.question: Where does this matter in an AI app?
followUps.html: Conversation IDs, selected run or trace, and filters in an evaluation dashboard belong in the URL so links can be shared and a refresh resumes the same view.

links.label: H7 Custom Hooks and the Rules of Hooks

react-q21.testing: tearing under concurrent rendering and the correct subscription primitive.
react-q21.spoken:
"It's the correct way to read from a store that lives outside React — a Redux or Zustand store, the browser's online status, matchMedia, the URL — and re-render when it changes.

The problem it solves is tearing. With concurrent rendering, React can pause a render halfway through a tree and yield to the browser. If the external store changes during that pause, components rendered before the pause show the old value and components rendered after show the new one — the same data displayed inconsistently in one frame. React can't prevent that for data it doesn't own.

useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot) gives React what it needs: a way to subscribe and a way to read the current snapshot. React checks the snapshot during render and, if it changed mid-render, re-renders synchronously so the whole tree is consistent. It also handles SSR via the server snapshot.

The older pattern — useState plus a subscription in useEffect — misses updates between render and effect and can tear. Library authors use this hook under the hood; application code uses it for browser APIs and custom stores."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "It lets React read an external store consistently across a whole render, even when rendering is interruptible."

stages.name: What React does
stages.claim: snapshot checks and forced sync re-render
stages.html:
Step Role
subscribe(cb) React registers to be told about changes
getSnapshot() read the current value; must return the same reference if unchanged
during/after render React compares snapshots; if changed mid-render, re-renders synchronously
getServerSnapshot() value used on the server and during hydration

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: two components, one store, consistent values
stages.html:
const store = { v: 0, subs: new Set(), set(n) { this.v = n; this.subs.forEach(f => f()) },
  subscribe(f) { store.subs.add(f); return () => store.subs.delete(f) }, get: () => store.v }
function A() { const v = useSyncExternalStore(store.subscribe, store.get); return <span>{v}</span> }
// render <A /><A />, then store.set(7)
// → "77", subscribers: 2            (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

Tearing itself needs a concurrent render interrupted mid-tree; it's hard to show in a few lines, which is why the guarantee matters.

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
• getSnapshot returning a new object each call → infinite re-render loop ("The result of getSnapshot should be cached").
  • Unstable subscribe function → resubscribes every render; define it outside the component or memoize.

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html: • 18: introduced with concurrent rendering (a shim exists for 16/17). State libraries (Redux, Zustand) adopted it.

followUps.question: getSnapshot = () => ({ online: navigator.onLine }). What happens?
followUps.html: React sees a new object on every call, assumes the store changed, and re-renders repeatedly — React warns about an uncached snapshot. Return the primitive navigator.onLine.

followUps.question: "A subscription in useEffect with useState works the same."
followUps.html: It can miss changes between render and effect and tear under concurrent rendering. useSyncExternalStore is the supported way.

followUps.question: What is tearing?
followUps.html: Different parts of the UI showing different versions of the same data in one committed frame, because the source changed during an interrupted render.

followUps.question: Should app code use it directly?
followUps.html: For browser APIs (online status, media queries, URL) and small custom stores, yes; for app state, use a library that already builds on it.

followUps.question: A real-time dashboard pushes prices via WebSocket into a store. How do you connect it to React?
followUps.html: Keep the socket outside React, write updates into a store with fine-grained selectors, read via useSyncExternalStore (or Zustand selectors), and throttle updates per frame so hundreds of messages don't cause hundreds of renders.

react-q22.testing: two independent reasons — parent re-render and context value identity — and which fix addresses which.
react-q22.trap: "memoize the context value" as the whole fix.
react-q22.spoken:
"There are two reasons, and they need different fixes.

The first is simpler: ExpensiveTree is rendered by App, and changing the theme re-renders App. By default React re-renders all children of a component that re-renders, whether or not their props changed. So as written, ExpensiveTree re-renders even without any context.

The second: the provider's value is { user, setUser }, a new object every time App renders. Context consumers re-render when the value changes identity, so even a memoized ExpensiveTree would still re-render, because its context changed by reference.

The fix needs both: memoize the value — useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]) — so it only changes when user changes, and stop the parent re-render from reaching the tree, either by wrapping ExpensiveTree in memo or by moving the theme state into its own component so App doesn't re-render. Splitting contexts helps further: theme and auth in separate providers, and state and setters in separate contexts."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function App() {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [theme, setTheme] = useState('dark');
  return (
    <AuthCtx.Provider value={{ user, setUser }}>
      <button onClick={() => setTheme(t => (t === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark'))} />
      <ExpensiveTree />
    </AuthCtx.Provider>
  );
}

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it — renders of the tree over mount + one theme change:

Setup Tree renders
as written (inline value, no memo) 2
memo(ExpensiveTree), inline value 2 (context identity changed)
memo(ExpensiveTree) + useMemo value 1
no memo, useMemo value 2 (parent re-render) 
// (React 19.3, jsdom harness; one theme click after mount)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: parent renders cascade; context compares by reference
stages.html:
• A re-rendering component re-renders its children unless they bail out (memo with equal props, or elements passed from above).
  • Context consumers re-render when value changes by Object.is, regardless of memo.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.html:
Variant Effect
move theme state into a ThemeToggle component App doesn't re-render on theme change
pass ExpensiveTree as children from above not re-created by the provider component
split AuthStateCtx / AuthDispatchCtx setter-only consumers never re-render for user changes

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • A single "AppContext" with an inline object re-renders every consumer on any change. Split by concern and update frequency; for high-frequency data, use a store with selectors (Q23).

followUps.question: You memoize the value with useMemo(..., [user]) but don't memo ExpensiveTree. Theme change: does it re-render?
followUps.html: Yes — measured: its parent App re-rendered, and a non-memoized child re-renders with it. The memoized value only helps components that would otherwise bail out.

followUps.question: "Memoize the context value and you're done."
followUps.html: Necessary but not sufficient: parent re-renders still cascade to non-memoized children.

followUps.question: Why split state and dispatch contexts?
followUps.html: Components that only call setUser don't need to re-render when user changes; a separate context with the stable setter gives them that.

followUps.question: Does context have selectors?
followUps.html: No: every consumer re-renders when the value changes. For selective subscriptions use a store (Zustand, Redux) or libraries like use-context-selector.

followUps.question: How would you find this in a real app?
followUps.html: React DevTools Profiler with "Why did this render?": it shows "context changed" vs "parent rendered". Fix accordingly and measure the commit time drop.

dontSay: Only one of the two causes.
"Context re-renders everything" without the identity detail.

links.label: ST2 Context Patterns and the Performance Cliff

react-q23.testing: Context as dependency injection, not a state manager, and its no-selector re-render model.
react-q23.spoken:
"Context is dependency injection for a subtree: it lets deeply nested components read a value without passing props through every level. It's great for values that change rarely and are needed widely: theme, locale, the current user, feature flags, and injecting services or clients — an API client, an analytics instance.

It's the wrong instinct for high-frequency or large state. Context has no selectors: when the value changes, every consumer re-renders, even if it only uses one field. Put a form's field values, a live cursor position or streaming tokens in context and the whole subtree re-renders on every change.

It's also the wrong instinct for server data — that belongs in a query cache — and for avoiding two levels of prop passing, where plain props or composition with children are clearer.

So I use context for stable, widely-needed values, split providers by update frequency, and use a store with selectors — Zustand, Redux — when many components need slices of frequently changing shared state."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: convenience of injection vs re-render cost
stages.html: "Context removes prop drilling; it doesn't give fine-grained subscriptions."

stages.name: Where Context wins
stages.html:
Good fit Why
theme, locale, auth user rare changes, many readers
service/client injection stable objects, testability
compound components (Tabs, Menu) scoped shared state within one widget

stages.name: Where it's the wrong instinct
stages.html:
Bad fit Better
high-frequency values store with selectors, local state
server data query cache
2–3 levels of props props or children composition
one giant AppContext split contexts by concern

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: how often does it change and how many read it?
stages.html:
Prove it — every consumer re-renders, even for fields it ignores:

const Ctx = createContext(null)
function Name() { const { user } = useContext(Ctx); renders.name++; return user }
function Cursor() { const { pos } = useContext(Ctx); renders.cursor++; return pos.x }
// value = { user, pos } updated 60×/s for mouse moves → Name re-renders 60×/s too

The pattern is the drill's point; measure with the Profiler on your own tree before and after splitting.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: context for stable values, stores for the rest
stages.html: • Context for theme/locale/auth/services; split providers; Zustand/Redux with selectors for shared client state; a query library for server state (Q24).

followUps.question: A provider's value is a memoized object that changes only when user changes. A consumer reads only setUser. Does it re-render when user changes?
followUps.html: Yes: the whole value changed identity. Split setUser into its own context to avoid it.

followUps.question: "Context replaces Redux."
followUps.html: It replaces prop drilling. Redux (or Zustand) adds selectors, middleware, devtools and predictable updates; context has none of those.

followUps.question: Is prop drilling bad?
followUps.html: A few levels are fine and explicit. Composition — passing components as children or props — often removes the drilling without context.

followUps.question: How do you test components that use context?
followUps.html: Render them with a test provider supplying fake values/services; that injection is one of context's strengths.

followUps.question: Where would you put streaming chat tokens?
followUps.html: Not in context: a per-conversation store or local state in the message list leaf, with tokens buffered per frame, so only the streaming message re-renders.

links.label: ST2 Context Patterns and the Performance Cliff

spine: What I'd pick for a real app
react-q24.testing: splitting state by category rather than picking one library.
react-q24.spoken:
"I don't pick one library; I split state by category, because each category has different needs.

Server state — data that lives on the server: users, orders, conversation history. It needs caching, deduplication, background refetching, invalidation after mutations, and loading and error states. That's a query library's job: TanStack Query, or in Next.js App Router, Server Components plus the framework cache. Most 'global state' in older Redux apps was actually this.

Shared client state — things the server doesn't know about but several distant components need: a draft that spans panels, a selection, UI preferences. For a small slice, Zustand: tiny API, selectors so components only re-render for what they read, no provider. Redux Toolkit when the org already standardises on it, when I want strict event-sourced updates and time-travel devtools, or many teams share one large, complex client state.

Local state stays local, in useState or useReducer. And state that should survive a refresh or be shareable — filters, tabs, selected IDs — goes in the URL.

Context plus useReducer is fine for low-frequency values like theme or auth, but it has no selectors.

So in a typical AI product I'd pick TanStack Query for conversations and runs, Zustand for the active composer and streaming UI state, the URL for the selected conversation, and local state for everything else."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: what kind of state is it?
stages.html:
Category Examples Tool
server state lists, records, history TanStack Query / RSC + framework cache
shared client state cross-panel drafts, selections Zustand (small) / Redux Toolkit (large, standardised)
local UI state open/closed, input value useState / useReducer
URL state filters, tabs, IDs search params
low-frequency globals theme, locale, auth Context

stages.name: Server state
stages.html: • Dedupe, stale-while-revalidate, invalidation after mutations, retries, pagination — built in.

stages.name: Shared client state
stages.html:
Prove it — a Zustand slice with selector-based subscriptions:

const useComposer = create(set => ({
  draft: '', streamingRunId: null,
  setDraft: draft => set({ draft }),
  startRun: id => set({ streamingRunId: id }),
}))
function SendButton() { const running = useComposer(s => s.streamingRunId !== null); return <button disabled={running}>Send</button> }
// 3 draft updates → SendButton renders stay at 1; startRun → 2   (React 19.3, zustand 5.0.15, jsdom harness)

stages.name: Local and URL state
stages.html: • Colocate by default; lift only as far as needed; URL for shareable state (Q20).

stages.name: What I'd pick for a real app
stages.html: • TanStack Query (conversations, runs, messages history), Zustand (composer, active stream UI), URL (selected conversation/run), local state (menus, inputs), Context (theme, auth).

followUps.question: Your Redux store holds users fetched from the API and you add a user via a form. What code do you write in Redux vs TanStack Query?
followUps.html: Redux: a thunk, pending/fulfilled/rejected reducers, manual cache update or refetch, stale handling. TanStack Query: a useMutation whose onSuccess calls invalidateQueries(['users']); the list refetches automatically.

followUps.question: "Redux is outdated."
followUps.html: Redux Toolkit is fine for large shared client state and teams wanting strict patterns and devtools. What's outdated is using it as a server cache.

followUps.question: Why Zustand over Context for shared state?
followUps.html: Selectors: components re-render only when their selected slice changes; no provider nesting; works outside React too.

followUps.question: Where does RTK Query fit?
followUps.html: It's Redux Toolkit's server-state layer — a reasonable choice if the app is already on Redux; otherwise TanStack Query is the common default.

followUps.question: How do you defend this to a team used to "everything in Redux"?
followUps.html: Show the boilerplate and bugs in server-data slices (stale data, missing invalidation), migrate one feature to a query library as a reference, and write the one-page rule of which state goes where (Q28).

dontSay: Server data in a client store by default.

links.label: ST4 Server State vs Client State

react-q25.testing: server state as a cache of data you don't own, and the features that implies.
react-q25.trap: "server state is just global state you fetched."
react-q25.spoken:
"Server state is data whose source of truth is on the server: you don't own it, other users and processes change it, and your copy is always a snapshot that may be stale. Client state is data the browser owns: a draft, an open panel.

Treating server state as client state — fetch once, put it in Redux — means hand-building everything a cache needs: loading and error states, deduplicating identical requests from several components, deciding when data is stale and refetching it — on focus, on reconnect, on an interval — invalidating after mutations, pagination, retries, garbage-collecting unused data. Every Redux app rebuilt those, inconsistently.

Query libraries like TanStack Query and SWR are caches keyed by the request: useQuery(['user', id], fetchUser). Components declare what they need; the library dedupes, caches, revalidates in the background, and tells you when data is stale. Mutations invalidate keys, and the right queries refetch.

That removed most of what global stores were holding, leaving them with genuine client state. In Next.js App Router, Server Components and the framework's data cache take part of this role too."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.claim: a local copy of remote truth
stages.html: "Server state is a cache of data you don't own; its core problem is freshness, not storage."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html:
Feature Hand-rolled in Redux Query library
dedupe identical requests manual automatic by key
stale-while-revalidate manual built in (staleTime)
refetch on focus/reconnect manual built in
invalidate after mutation manual invalidateQueries(key)
GC of unused data rarely done gcTime
race handling manual (Q13) per key

stages.name: Where it breaks
stages.html:
Prove it — the whole data layer for a list and a mutation:

function Users() {
  const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['users'], queryFn: fetchUsers, staleTime: 30_000 })
  const qc = useQueryClient()
  const add = useMutation({ mutationFn: createUser, onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['users'] }) })
  if (isPending) return <Spinner />
  if (error) return <ErrorView error={error} />
  return <List users={data} onAdd={add.mutate} />
}
  • Breaks when keys are inconsistent (the same data under two keys), staleTime is wrong for the data, or you mirror query data into another store.

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.claim: staleTime per resource, no API data in Redux
stages.html: • Dashboards and admin tools: staleTime per resource, prefetch on hover, optimistic updates for quick actions (Q26), and no server data in Redux.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • In App Router, many reads move to the server (RSC fetch + cache); client query libraries remain for interactive, client-driven data (Q37).

followUps.question: Three components call useQuery(['user', 42]) at the same time. How many network requests?
followUps.html: One: identical keys are deduplicated; all three subscribe to the same cache entry.

followUps.question: "Server state is just global state."
followUps.html: It's global and stale by nature; the hard part is freshness and invalidation, which global stores don't address.

followUps.question: What does staleTime vs gcTime mean?
followUps.html: staleTime: how long data counts as fresh (no background refetch). gcTime: how long unused data stays in memory after the last subscriber unmounts.

followUps.question: Should you copy query data into Zustand?
followUps.html: No: that creates a second source of truth that won't refetch or invalidate. Derive from the query or select from it.

followUps.question: How does this apply to an AI chat app?
followUps.html: Conversation history and run status are server state (queries, invalidated on completion); the currently streaming message is client state until the run finishes, then the query cache takes over.

react-q26.testing: rollback correctness and out-of-order concurrent mutations.
react-q26.trap: optimistic UI with no failure path.
react-q26.spoken:
"An optimistic update shows the expected result immediately — the like count goes up, the item appears in the list — before the server confirms, then reconciles with the server's response. It makes the UI feel instant for actions that almost always succeed.

The two ways it bites.

First, rollback. If the request fails, you must restore exactly the state before the change and tell the user. Naive code restores the wrong thing — for example a snapshot taken before a second mutation, wiping that one out — or doesn't roll back at all, so the UI shows data the server never accepted.

Second, out-of-order concurrent mutations. The user clicks like, unlike, like quickly. Three requests are in flight; responses can arrive in any order, and if each response overwrites local state, the UI settles on whichever came back last, not what the user last did. Fixes: serialise mutations per entity, send the intended final state rather than a toggle, use idempotency keys, and after mutations settle, refetch to converge on the server's truth.

In React 19, useOptimistic handles the display side inside transitions and reverts automatically when the action finishes; TanStack Query's onMutate/onError/onSettled handles the cache side."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: show the expected result, reconcile later
stages.html: "Optimistic UI predicts the server's answer; correctness depends on rollback and ordering."

stages.name: How it works
Prove it
stages.html:
useMutation({
  mutationFn: toggleLike,
  onMutate: async ({ postId, liked }) => {
    await qc.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] })
    const prev = qc.getQueryData(['post', postId])
    qc.setQueryData(['post', postId], p => ({ ...p, liked, likes: p.likes + (liked ? 1 : -1) }))
    return { prev }
  },
  onError: (_e, { postId }, ctx) => qc.setQueryData(['post', postId], ctx.prev),
  onSettled: (_d, _e, { postId }) => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['post', postId] }),
})

stages.name: Where it bites
stages.html:
Bite Symptom Guard
rollback UI shows unsaved data, or rollback wipes another change per-mutation snapshots, invalidate on settle, error toast
out-of-order responses final state ≠ user's last action send absolute state (liked: true), serialise per entity, idempotency keys, refetch on settle

stages.name: What changed by version
stages.html: • React 19: useOptimistic(state, updateFn) shows optimistic state during an action/transition and falls back to real state when it settles.

followUps.question: 🧪 User clicks Like (request A, slow), then Unlike (request B, fast). B succeeds, then A succeeds. With toggle semantics, what's the final server state?
followUps.html: Depends on server arrival order, not click order: if A is processed after B, the post ends liked though the user unliked. Send absolute intent (liked: false) and sequence or serialise mutations per post.

followUps.question: "Optimistic updates are just setting state early."
followUps.html: That's the easy half. The design is the failure and ordering path; without it, optimistic UI shows data the server rejected.

followUps.question: When shouldn't you be optimistic?
followUps.html: Actions that often fail validation, money movements, irreversible actions, or where the server computes the result (prices, IDs) — show pending state instead.

followUps.question: Why cancel in-flight queries in onMutate?
followUps.html: So a refetch started earlier doesn't land after your optimistic write and overwrite it with stale server data.

followUps.question: In an AI chat, is sending a message optimistic?
followUps.html: The user's message can appear immediately with a pending marker and a client ID; the assistant's reply can't be predicted, so it streams. On failure, mark the message with a retry action rather than removing it.

react-q27.testing: explicit transitions, testable pure logic, and a stable dispatch.
react-q27.trap: "useReducer is for big state, useState for small."
react-q27.spoken:
"Mechanically they're the same thing — useState is implemented with a reducer. What useReducer buys is structure.

Transitions become explicit: instead of scattered setX, setY calls in handlers that must stay consistent, you dispatch named events — 'submitStarted', 'submitFailed' — and one pure function decides how every field changes. That makes impossible states harder to create, like loading: true with an error still set, and the reducer is testable without rendering anything.

And dispatch is stable across renders, so it can go into effect dependencies or down to memoized children without useCallback.

useState stays better for independent, simple values. I switch to a reducer when several fields change together or the next state depends on the current state in non-trivial ways — forms with async submission, wizards, a chat composer's run lifecycle."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: scattered setters vs one transition function
stages.html: "Same engine; useReducer centralises how state changes."

stages.name: Where useState wins
stages.html: • A toggle, an input value, a selected tab.

stages.name: Where useReducer wins
stages.html:
Prove it — a pure, testable transition function:

function submitReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'start':   return { status: 'submitting', error: null }
    case 'success': return { status: 'done', error: null }
    case 'fail':    return { status: 'idle', error: action.error }
    default:        return state
  }
}
console.log(submitReducer({ status: 'submitting', error: 'x' }, { type: 'success' }))
// → { status: 'done', error: null }    (plain JS, no React needed)

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html: • Yes, or transitions have rules → reducer. No → useState.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: reducers for lifecycles, useState for the rest
stages.html: • Reducer for async forms, wizards, streaming run state (idle → streaming → done | error | aborted); useState elsewhere; a store when the state must be shared widely.

followUps.question: Is dispatch a new function on each render?
followUps.html: No: React guarantees dispatch (like setState) is stable for the component's lifetime, so it's safe in dependency arrays.

followUps.question: "useReducer is for complex/large state."
followUps.html: It's for coupled transitions, not size. A big object of independent fields may be fine with several useStates.

followUps.question: Can reducers have side effects?
followUps.html: No: they must be pure (React may call them twice in StrictMode). Side effects go in handlers or effects that react to state.

followUps.question: useReducer + Context — is that Redux?
followUps.html: A small version of it, without selectors, middleware or devtools; fine for low-frequency shared state.

followUps.question: How would you model a streaming AI run?
followUps.html: A reducer with events start, token, toolCall, done, error, abort; states make illegal combinations (tokens after done) impossible, and the reducer is unit-tested with recorded event sequences.

react-q28.testing: classify before refactoring, a written rule, and incremental strangling with guardrails.
react-q28.trap: proposing a rewrite or a new library.
react-q28.spoken:
"I'd classify before I refactor. First an inventory: for each piece of state — users, cart, filters, drafts — where is it held, who writes it, and how many copies exist. That usually shows most of the swamp is server data copied into Redux and Context, with URL-worthy state like filters living in three places.

Then a one-page rule the team agrees on: server data lives in the query cache; shared client state lives in one store; local state stays local; shareable state goes in the URL; Context only for low-frequency globals like theme and auth. Every piece of state has exactly one owner.

Then strangle it, one vertical feature at a time rather than by layer. Pick a feature with obvious pain, migrate it completely to the rule, and make it the reference implementation others copy. New code must follow the rule, enforced by lint: for example, a lint rule or import restriction that blocks new usage of the old Redux slices, with a list of deprecated paths.

To keep it safe: characterization tests on the migrated flows before touching them, feature flags if behaviour changes, and a migration dashboard — slices remaining, copies removed. With 40 contributors, the social part matters as much as the code: an RFC, office hours, and a named owner for the state architecture."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
State Holders today Category Target owner
current user Redux + AuthContext server + auth query cache (+ auth context for session)
orders list Redux slice + component state server query cache
filters Redux + URL + local URL-worthy URL
editor draft Context + local shared client one store

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • Features keep shipping; migration must be incremental and reversible; rules must be enforceable automatically.

stages.name: Baseline plan
Deep-dive
stages.html:
Prove it — an ESLint guard on deprecated state paths:

// .eslintrc — block new imports of legacy slices outside allow-listed files
rules: {
  'no-restricted-imports': ['error', { paths: [
    { name: '@/store/ordersSlice', message: 'Use useOrdersQuery() — see docs/state-rules.md' },
  ] }],
}
  • Plus: codemods for mechanical moves, CODEOWNERS on the state layer, a dashboard counting remaining usages.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: rewrites stall, new libraries add copies
stages.html: • Big-bang rewrite stalls; a new library added as "the fix" becomes a fourth copy (Q44); migrating by layer leaves every feature half-migrated; no tests → behaviour regressions.

stages.name: What I'd measure
stages.html: • Count of duplicated state sources, legacy import usages over time, bug rate in migrated features, and developer feedback on the rule.

followUps.question: After migrating orders to TanStack Query, an old component still reads state.orders from Redux. What happens after a user creates an order?
followUps.html: The query cache is invalidated and refetched, but the Redux copy is stale, so that component shows old data — the duplicate-source bug. Migrate or bridge that component and delete the slice.

followUps.question: "Rewrite state management from scratch."
followUps.html: Rewrites stall under continuing feature work and break behaviour nobody documented. Incremental migration with a reference implementation ships value each step.

followUps.question: Why migrate by vertical feature?
followUps.html: A fully migrated feature is a working example, removes duplication end to end, and can be verified; layer-by-layer leaves everything half-done.

followUps.question: How do you get 40 people to follow the rule?
followUps.html: Make the right way easiest: a reference implementation, generators/templates, lint errors on the old way, and review checklists.

followUps.question: How long and how do you report progress?
followUps.html: Quarter-scale for a large app; report legacy usage counts trending down, incidents related to stale data, and feature velocity — so leadership sees it as risk reduction, not refactoring for its own sake.

react-q29.testing: profile first, reason about why each component rendered, structural fixes before memo.
react-q29.spoken:
"I start by measuring, with the React DevTools Profiler recording while I type, and the 'why did this render' option on. That tells me, per component, whether it rendered because its own state changed, its parent rendered, a prop changed, or a context changed — and how long each commit took. The Chrome Performance panel shows whether keystrokes create long tasks, which is what INP measures.

Then I decide whether the problem is breadth — many components rendering — or depth — a few components doing expensive work.

The usual cause of breadth is state living too high: the search input's value is stored in a page-level component or a context, so every keystroke re-renders the whole page. The fix is moving the input state down into the search box component, and passing only the committed query up, or using composition so the expensive parts are passed as children.

For the results list, which genuinely depends on the query, I'd keep the input urgent and render the results as non-urgent with useDeferredValue or useTransition, so typing stays responsive while the list catches up. If the list is long, virtualise it.

Memoization comes after that, targeted at components the profiler shows as costly, with stable props. Then I re-measure to prove the improvement — commit time per keystroke and INP."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html: • Poor INP on the search page; each keystroke causes a long task.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.html:
Tool What it shows
React DevTools Profiler + "why did this render" which components, why, how long
Chrome Performance panel long tasks per keystroke
web-vitals INP (field) real users' interaction latency

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Profiler says Suspect Fix
"parent rendered" ×60 state too high move state down / composition
"context changed" input value in context local state; split context
one component 40 ms expensive render memoize calculation, virtualise
results list slow urgent + heavy together useDeferredValue

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it — state moved down, results deferred:

function SearchPage() {                      // no longer holds keystroke state
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)
  return <><SearchBox onChange={setQuery} /><Results query={deferred} /><Sidebar /><Feed /></>
}
const Results = memo(function Results({ query }) { /* expensive filtering + list */ })
  • Typing updates query urgently; Results re-renders with the deferred value in a lower-priority pass that yields to new keystrokes. Sidebar and Feed still re-render with SearchPage unless the input state moves into SearchBox itself.

stages.name: Fix
stages.html: 1. Move state down / composition. 2. useDeferredValue or useTransition for heavy dependents. 3. Virtualise long lists. 4. Targeted memo with stable props. 5. React Compiler where adopted.

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.claim: INP by route and render-count tests
stages.html: • INP in field monitoring by route; a performance test recording render counts for key interactions; review rule on where input state lives.

followUps.question: The input's value lives in a Context read by 60 components. You wrap all 60 in memo. Does it help?
followUps.html: No: context consumers re-render when the context value changes, regardless of memo. Move the input value out of the context.

followUps.question: "memo everything, then profile."
followUps.html: Backwards: profile first, fix structure, then memo the few proven hot spots.

followUps.question: useDeferredValue vs debounce?
followUps.html: Debounce delays work by a fixed time even on fast devices; useDeferredValue renders as soon as there's time and interrupts stale work, adapting to the device. Debounce still helps for network requests.

followUps.question: How do you prove the fix to others?
followUps.html: Before/after Profiler commit durations and render counts per keystroke, and INP p75 from field data after release.

followUps.question: Same symptom in a chat input while a response streams. Cause and fix?
followUps.html: Streaming tokens update state high in the tree, re-rendering the composer on every token. Isolate the streaming message in its own leaf fed by a per-frame buffer, keep composer state local, and defer the transcript list.

react-q30.testing: state is preserved by type + position; a key creates a new identity.
react-q30.trap: answer A — resetting with an effect.
react-q30.spoken:
"B: render <Editor key={docId} docId={selectedId} />.

React preserves a component's state as long as the same component type sits at the same position in the tree. Switching docId only changes a prop, so the Editor instance — and its draft state — survives.

Giving it key={docId} tells React each document is a different instance: when the key changes, React unmounts the old editor and mounts a fresh one with fresh state. That's cleaner than option A, an effect that clears the draft, which renders once with the stale draft, then again cleared, and must be kept in sync with every new piece of state."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Editor({ docId }) {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState('');
  return <textarea value={draft} onChange={e => setDraft(e.target.value)} />;
}
// parent
<Editor docId={selectedId} />
  • A: add useEffect(() => setDraft(''), [docId]) · B: render <Editor key={docId} docId={selectedId} /> · C: move draft to the parent · D: wrap Editor in React.memo

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// type "draft for a" in doc a, then switch to doc b
// → without key: "draft for a"
// → key={docId}: ""                 (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html: • Props changing never resets state; a new key does (Q4).

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: the effect and memo options fall short
stages.html:
Option Result
A: effect resets works, but an extra render with the stale draft and fragile as state grows
B: key fresh instance, all state reset
C: lift draft to parent works if the parent stores drafts per doc (e.g. a map) — useful to keep unsaved drafts
D: memo no effect on state

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Record detail panes, chat composers per conversation, forms per selected item: key by the record ID. If drafts must survive switching, store them in a map keyed by ID instead.

followUps.question: With key={docId}, the Editor also has an expensive useMemo. What happens on switch?
followUps.html: It recomputes: the new instance has no cached memo. Usually fine; if not, cache per doc outside the component.

followUps.question: "Use an effect to reset the state when the prop changes."
followUps.html: It renders the stale state first, then resets — a flash and an extra render — and must be updated for every new piece of state. A key resets all of it correctly.

followUps.question: Does a key remount the DOM too?
followUps.html: Yes: the old DOM subtree is removed and a new one created, so focus and scroll inside it reset as well.

followUps.question: When would you choose option C?
followUps.html: When users expect unsaved drafts per document to survive switching: store drafts[docId] in the parent or a store.

followUps.question: In a chat app, conversation A's half-typed message appears in conversation B. Fix?
followUps.html: <Composer key={conversationId} /> for a clean slate, or a draft store keyed by conversation ID if drafts should persist per conversation.

react-q31.testing: rendering less beats rendering faster; knowing virtualisation's costs.
react-q31.spoken:
"The fastest row is the one you never render. With 10,000 rows, the DOM itself — 10,000 rows times several cells — is the cost: layout, style recalculation and memory, before React is even involved.

Option one, virtualisation: render only the rows in the viewport plus a small overscan, with TanStack Virtual or react-window, and recycle them as you scroll. That turns tens of thousands of nodes into a few dozen. Trade-offs: variable row heights need measuring, find-in-page and printing don't see off-screen rows, accessibility needs care — aria-rowcount and aria-rowindex — and sticky headers or column resizing get more complex.

Option two, do less on the client: server-side pagination, filtering and sorting, so the browser never has 10,000 rows. Trade-off: every interaction is a request, so it needs good loading states and a query cache.

Option three, cheaper rows: memoized row components with stable props, no heavy formatting in render, CSS content-visibility: auto for simpler lists. These are the smallest wins.

My pick: virtualise the table, push filtering and sorting to the server if the data is truly large, and profile before touching row-level memoization."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "Reduce the number of DOM nodes before optimising each one."

stages.name: Virtualisation
stages.html:
Prove it — the node arithmetic (illustrative):

10,000 rows × 8 cells = 80,000 cells (+ wrappers) in the DOM
Viewport 800 px / 36 px rows ≈ 23 visible + 10 overscan ≈ 33 rows × 8 = 264 cells
→ ~300× fewer nodes to lay out and style
Cost Mitigation
variable heights measure rows (dynamic virtualisers)
Ctrl+F / print provide search in-app; print view
accessibility role="grid", aria-rowcount, keyboard navigation

stages.name: Server-side pagination and filtering
stages.html: • Cursor pagination, server sort/filter, prefetch the next page, keep previous page visible during loading.

stages.name: Cheaper rows
stages.html: • memo rows with stable props (ids, not objects); precompute formatted values; avoid inline heavy components per cell; content-visibility: auto for non-virtualised lists.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: virtualise, and let the server filter
stages.html: • Virtualised grid + server-side sort/filter for big datasets; profile scroll with the Performance panel (frame rate, long tasks) before and after.

followUps.question: 🧪 After virtualising, a user presses Ctrl+F for a value in row 9,000. What happens?
followUps.html: The browser can't find it: that row isn't in the DOM. Provide an in-app search/filter that scrolls to the matching row.

followUps.question: "memo every row and it'll be smooth."
followUps.html: Memo reduces React re-renders, not the cost of 80,000 DOM nodes on scroll. Virtualise first.

followUps.question: Why is scroll janky even without re-renders?
followUps.html: Layout, painting and memory for a huge DOM; scroll handlers doing work; images loading. Rendering less DOM fixes the base cost.

followUps.question: Pagination or infinite scroll?
followUps.html: Pagination for tables users navigate and reference ("page 3"); infinite scroll for feeds. Either way, virtualise long loaded lists.

followUps.question: A log viewer streams 50 new lines per second into a list. Design?
followUps.html: Virtualised list, buffered appends flushed per animation frame, a cap on retained lines (ring buffer) with "load older" from the server, and auto-scroll only when the user is at the bottom.

dontSay: Shipping 10,000 rows when the server can filter.

links.label: D4 Large Lists and Noisy Input

react-q32.testing: splitting where it pays, and hiding the latency you introduced.
react-q32.trap: splitting everything into tiny chunks that load in a waterfall with spinners.
react-q32.spoken:
"I split where the code isn't needed for the first screen, at three kinds of boundary. Routes: each page's code loads when you navigate there — frameworks like Next.js do this automatically. On-intent surfaces: modals, editors, settings panels, charts — things behind a click. And heavy vendor libraries used in one place: a rich-text editor, a PDF viewer, a charting library.

Splitting adds latency at the moment the user asks for the feature, so I hide it. Prefetch on intent: start loading the chunk on hover or focus of the button, or when the route link enters the viewport. Keep the old screen visible: wrap the navigation or state change in a transition so React keeps showing the current UI instead of flashing a spinner, and put Suspense boundaries where a loading state makes sense to the user, with skeletons matching the final layout.

What I avoid: splitting small components, which adds requests without saving much; nested lazy components that load in a waterfall; and splitting things needed for the first paint. I verify with a bundle analyzer and by watching the network waterfall on a throttled connection."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Everything needed for the initial route's first paint stays in the main chunk; everything else is a candidate.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • Each split point adds a request when first used; on slow networks that's visible.

stages.name: Baseline boundaries
stages.html:
Prove it — lazy + prefetch on intent + transition:

const loadEditor = () => import('./RichEditor')
const RichEditor = lazy(loadEditor)
function EditButton() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)
  const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
  return <>
    <button onMouseEnter={loadEditor} onFocus={loadEditor} onClick={() => startTransition(() => setOpen(true))}>
      {isPending ? 'Opening…' : 'Edit'}
    </button>
    {open && <Suspense fallback={<EditorSkeleton />}><RichEditor /></Suspense>}
  </>
}

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Boundary Payoff
routes biggest, automatic in frameworks
modals/editors/settings large, rarely used code
heavy libraries (charts, PDF, maps) large vendor chunks
small shared components negative: extra requests

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Spinner flashes on every interaction; waterfalls of nested lazy chunks; duplicated vendor code across chunks; splitting first-screen code (worse LCP).

stages.name: What I'd measure
stages.claim: JS per route and a CI budget
stages.html: • JS per route (bundle analyzer), LCP and INP in the field, time-to-open for split features on a throttled network, and a CI bundle-size budget.

followUps.question: A lazy modal is opened with plain setOpen(true) (no transition) inside an existing Suspense boundary high up the tree. What does the user see?
followUps.html: The nearest Suspense fallback shows — possibly replacing a large part of the page with a spinner — until the chunk loads. A transition keeps the current UI visible; a Suspense boundary close to the modal limits what's replaced.

followUps.question: "Split every component for the smallest bundle."
followUps.html: Tiny chunks add request overhead and waterfalls; total bytes barely change. Split at meaningful boundaries.

followUps.question: How does Next.js App Router change this?
followUps.html: Routes are split automatically; Server Components don't ship their code at all; next/dynamic for client-only heavy components; link prefetching in the viewport.

followUps.question: How do you find what to split?
followUps.html: A bundle analyzer on the production build, looking for large modules in the main chunk that aren't used on the first screen.

followUps.question: How do you keep bundles from growing back?
followUps.html: A per-route size budget in CI (e.g. size-limit), review of new heavy dependencies, and a dashboard of JS per route over time.

react-q33.testing: the Rules of Hooks and how React detects violations.
react-q33.trap: answering from the rule alone. Measured on React 19.3, this exact snippet doesn't throw — the drill's key (B) is wrong for it.
react-q33.spoken:
"The code breaks the Rules of Hooks — the early return makes useState conditional — so the linter flags it. But what actually happens at runtime is subtler than 'it throws', and I checked it on React 19.3.

React's runtime check compares hook counts between renders, and it only fires when at least one hook ran before the early return. Here no hook runs before the return, so going from "42" to null renders <Login /> without an error, and the name state is discarded: when userId comes back, the input starts empty.

Add a hook above the early return — say a useContext or useState — and it does throw: 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement', and in the other direction 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render'.

So the correct answer to this exact snippet is A — it renders <Login /> and the state is gone. The fix is the same either way: hooks above any early return, or split the branch into its own component so each has a fixed hook list."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
function Profile({ userId }) {
  if (!userId) return <Login />;
  const [name, setName] = useState('');
  return <input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />;
}
  • A: renders <Login /> fine, state is discarded · B: throws — "Rendered fewer hooks than expected" · C: name silently becomes undefined · D: React warns in dev, works in prod

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it — four variants on React 19.3 (jsdom harness):

Variant Sequence Result
this snippet (no hook before return) "42" → null no error; renders login
this snippet null → "42" no error; renders input
this snippet, typed "typed" "42" → null → "42" input comes back empty (state discarded)
hook before the return "42" → null throws Rendered fewer hooks than expected…
hook before the return null → "42" throws Rendered more hooks than during the previous render.

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: hooks are slot-indexed; the check needs a partial list
stages.html: • Hooks are matched by call order (Q7). React detects "too few" when the render stopped partway through the previous list; a render that calls zero hooks isn't caught, and the component's hook state is simply cleared.

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: one hook above the return makes it throw
stages.html:
• Any hook above the if → throws in both directions (table above).
  • Split: function Profile({ userId }) { return userId ? <ProfileForm /> : <Login /> } — each component has a fixed hook list; ProfileForm's state resets naturally when it unmounts.

stages.name: The production version
stages.claim: silent state loss is worse than a crash
stages.html: • The non-throwing case loses user input silently. Rely on eslint-plugin-react-hooks (rules-of-hooks: error), not on runtime errors.

followUps.question: Add const theme = useContext(ThemeCtx) as the first line. Now what happens on "42" → null?
followUps.html: It throws: "Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement." — one hook ran, then the render stopped short of the previous count.

followUps.question: "It always throws; that's what the rules of hooks are for."
followUps.html: The runtime check doesn't catch every violation — this exact snippet renders without error on React 19.3 and silently drops state. The lint rule is the real guard.

followUps.question: Why does the zero-hook render slip through?
followUps.html: The "fewer hooks" check triggers when a render ends partway through the previous hook list. With no hooks called at all there's no partial list to compare, and the component's hook state is reset.

followUps.question: What's the idiomatic fix?
followUps.html: Move all hooks above the early return, or split the conditional UI into separate components.

followUps.question: What would you tell the team after finding this?
followUps.html: Make rules-of-hooks an error in CI, don't rely on runtime errors or manual review, and treat "the app didn't crash" as no evidence of correctness for hooks code.

dontSay: "It always throws" (not for this snippet on 19.3).
