react-q34.testing: field data (RUM) over lab data, the right metrics, segmentation and guardrails.
react-q34.spoken:
"Field data, not lab data. My laptop is fast, on a good network, with a warm cache; users aren't. So I collect real-user metrics.

The core is web-vitals in the app, sending Core Web Vitals to our analytics: INP for interaction responsiveness — which is where React re-render problems show up — LCP for loading, and CLS for layout stability. I report them at the 75th percentile and segment by route, device class, connection type and country, because averages hide the slow devices where problems live. INP attribution tells me which interaction and which element was slow.

For React-specific cost, the <Profiler> component's onRender callback can sample commit durations for key subtrees in production — sampled, because it adds overhead — and long-animation-frame data shows which scripts block interactions.

Lab tools still matter as guards: Lighthouse CI and a bundle-size budget on every pull request, so regressions are caught before release. Then the field data confirms, and dashboards per route catch the regressions that tests don't."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Key routes and interactions (search, checkout, chat send); target percentiles and devices.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.claim: real devices are slow and varied
stages.html: • Mid-range Android on 4G is a very different world from a developer laptop; field data captures it.

stages.name: Baseline setup
stages.html:
Prove it — reporting INP with attribution:

import { onINP, onLCP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals/attribution'
function send(metric) {
  navigator.sendBeacon('/rum', JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name, value: metric.value, route: location.pathname,
    target: metric.attribution?.interactionTarget, device: navigator.hardwareConcurrency,
  }))
}
onINP(send); onLCP(send); onCLS(send)

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Metric Measures "Good" threshold (Google)
INP interaction → next paint ≤ 200 ms
LCP largest content visible ≤ 2.5 s
CLS layout shifts ≤ 0.1
React <Profiler> commit time (sampled) render cost of subtrees your budget
  • Segment by route, device, network; report p75, not averages.

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Lab-only measurement; averages; no segmentation; Profiler on for everyone (overhead); dashboards nobody watches.

stages.name: What I'd alert on
stages.html: • INP/LCP p75 regressions per route after deploys, bundle budget failures in CI, and long-animation-frame spikes.

followUps.question: 🧪 Lighthouse shows 98 on your laptop; field INP p75 is 450 ms. Which do you believe?
followUps.html: The field data: it's real users. Lighthouse lab doesn't measure real interactions and runs on your hardware. Use INP attribution to find the slow interactions.

followUps.question: "Lighthouse score is our performance metric."
followUps.html: It's a synthetic lab score; good for CI guards, not for how users experience the app.

followUps.question: Why p75?
followUps.html: It reflects most users' experience while not being dominated by extreme outliers; it's also what Core Web Vitals assessment uses.

followUps.question: Is the React Profiler safe in production?
followUps.html: The <Profiler> API works in production builds (with profiling enabled for detailed timings) but has overhead — sample it on a small share of sessions.

followUps.question: For an AI chat app, what extra metric would you add?
followUps.html: Time to first token as experienced in the browser, token render smoothness (frames dropped while streaming), and INP of the send action during a stream.

react-q35.testing: the user-visible effect: responsiveness under heavy renders, no jarring fallbacks.
react-q35.trap: "it makes rendering faster" or "it renders in parallel threads".
react-q35.spoken:
"The user-visible win is that urgent updates stay responsive while expensive ones happen in the background. Typing into a search box stays smooth even though the results list re-renders heavily, because React can interrupt the heavy render to handle the keystroke, then resume.

The second win is that transitions can keep the current screen visible instead of flashing a spinner: when you navigate or switch tabs and the new content isn't ready, React keeps showing the old content, with a pending indicator, until the new one is ready.

It doesn't make any render faster, and it's not parallel threads — it's the same JavaScript thread, just interruptible and prioritised. You opt in through transitions, deferred values and Suspense."

stages.name: Plain definition
stages.html: "Urgent updates jump the queue; heavy renders yield."

stages.name: Mechanism
stages.html: • Updates get priorities (lanes); transition renders check periodically whether to yield to the browser or to more urgent work; interrupted work is discarded and redone with fresh state.

stages.name: Where it doesn't help
stages.claim: single heavy renders and slow effects
stages.html:
Doesn't help Why
one huge synchronous computation in render can't be split mid-function
slow effects run outside the render phase
network latency still waiting
urgent updates that are heavy themselves they aren't deferred

Prove it — the opt-in:

const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)       // urgent: input; background: results
return <><input value={query} onChange={e => setQuery(e.target.value)} /><Results q={deferred} /></>

stages.name: How I've used it
stages.html: • Search-as-you-type with heavy results, tab switches that keep the old tab until data arrives, filtering large dashboards.

stages.name: Adjacent concept
stages.html: • Transitions decide whether a suspended update shows a fallback or keeps the old UI (Q36).

followUps.question: A Results component takes 300 ms to render and isn't split into smaller components. Does useDeferredValue keep typing smooth?
followUps.html: Partly at best: React yields between components, not inside one function. A single 300 ms component still blocks; split the work or reduce it (virtualise, memoize calculations).

followUps.question: "Concurrent React renders in parallel on multiple threads."
followUps.html: It's single-threaded; concurrency means interleaving and priorities, not parallelism.

followUps.question: Do I get it automatically?
followUps.html: createRoot enables the concurrent renderer, but updates are urgent by default; you opt specific updates into non-urgent via transitions and deferred values.

followUps.question: What does "tearing" have to do with this?
followUps.html: Interruptible rendering can observe external stores at different moments; useSyncExternalStore prevents inconsistent UI (Q21).

followUps.question: How does it help an AI chat UI?
followUps.html: Rendering the transcript's markdown and code highlighting as non-urgent keeps the composer and scroll responsive while tokens stream in.

react-q36.testing: same idea, different handle — who owns the state update.
react-q36.spoken:
"Both mark work as non-urgent so the current UI stays responsive; the difference is where you have a handle.

useTransition wraps the state update: startTransition(() => setTab(next)). I use it when I own the setter — navigation, tab switches, filters — and it gives me isPending to show a subtle indicator while the old UI stays on screen. In React 19 it can also wrap async functions, which is the basis for Actions.

useDeferredValue wraps a value: const deferred = useDeferredValue(query). I use it when I only receive the value — a prop, or state owned elsewhere — and want an expensive child to render with a lagging copy while the input stays urgent. I can compare query !== deferred to show that results are stale.

Neither is a debounce: they don't wait a fixed time; they render as soon as there's capacity and discard outdated work."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: wrap the update or wrap the value
stages.html:
useTransition useDeferredValue
you control the setter only the value
pending signal isPending value !== deferred
async (19) yes (Actions) —

stages.name: Where useTransition wins
stages.html:
Prove it — keep the old tab visible:

const [tab, setTab] = useState('about')
const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition()
<button onClick={() => startTransition(() => setTab('posts'))}>Posts{isPending && ' …'}</button>
<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><TabPanel tab={tab} /></Suspense>
// if Posts suspends, the About panel stays visible instead of the Spinner

stages.name: Where useDeferredValue wins
stages.html:
function Results({ query }) {                        // query is a prop
  const deferred = useDeferredValue(query)
  const stale = query !== deferred
  return <div style={{ opacity: stale ? 0.6 : 1 }}><HeavyList q={deferred} /></div>
}

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: do you own the state update?
stages.html: • Yes → useTransition. No → useDeferredValue.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: transitions for updates, deferred values for props
stages.html: • Tabs, navigation, filter changes: transition. Search results downstream of an input: deferred value. Network requests: still debounce or use a query library.

followUps.question: You wrap setQuery for a controlled input in startTransition. What happens when typing?
followUps.html: The input itself becomes non-urgent and can lag or feel sticky, because its displayed value updates at low priority. Keep the input state urgent and defer the expensive consumer.

followUps.question: "They're a built-in debounce."
followUps.html: No fixed delay: they render as soon as possible and discard outdated renders. Debounce is still useful for limiting network requests.

followUps.question: What does React 19 add to transitions?
followUps.html: Async transitions: startTransition(async () => { await save(); setX(...) }), with isPending covering the whole async action — the basis of Actions and useActionState.

followUps.question: Do they help data fetching?
followUps.html: With Suspense-enabled data they avoid replacing content with fallbacks; they don't make the fetch faster.

followUps.question: Where in an AI app?
followUps.html: Switching conversations (transition keeps the current one visible until the next loads), and rendering heavy markdown/code blocks from a streaming message with a deferred value so scrolling stays smooth.

dontSay: Picking by preference, not by who owns the update.

react-q37.testing: the RSC payload vs code, the client boundary, and serialisation rules.
react-q37.spoken:
"A Server Component runs only on the server — at build time or per request — and its code never ships to the browser. What ships is its output: a serialised description of the rendered tree, the RSC payload, with placeholders where Client Components go, plus the JavaScript for those Client Components only.

That gives two big wins. Zero bundle cost for server-only code: a markdown parser, a database client, a large date library used in a Server Component adds nothing to the client bundle. And data access where the data is: a Server Component can be async and await the database or an internal API directly, without a client-side fetch waterfall or an API endpoint just for the UI.

What you can't do in one follows from 'it already finished running on the server': no state, no effects, no event handlers, no browser APIs, no context consumption. Anything interactive goes in a Client Component, marked with 'use client', which is the boundary: everything it imports is client code.

Props crossing from server to client must be serialisable — plain data, not functions or class instances — except Server Actions, which are passed as references.

It's not the same as SSR: SSR turns components into HTML for the first load; RSC decides which components ever run on the client. In Next.js they're used together."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "Server Components send a serialised render result, not their JavaScript; only Client Components ship code."

stages.name: What ships
stages.claim: a payload plus client component code
stages.html:
Item Ships to browser?
Server Component code and its imports no
RSC payload (rendered tree, props for client components) yes
Client Component code ('use client' and its imports) yes
HTML for first load (via SSR) yes

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
// app/posts/page.jsx — Server Component (default in App Router)
import { db } from '@/lib/db'                 // never bundled for the client
import { marked } from 'marked'               // never bundled for the client
import LikeButton from './LikeButton'         // 'use client' inside
export default async function Posts() {
  const posts = await db.post.findMany()
  return posts.map(p => (
    <article key={p.id}>
      <div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: marked(p.body) }} />
      <LikeButton postId={p.id} />                {/* only this ships JS */}
    </article>
  ))
}
// LikeButton.jsx
'use client'
export default function LikeButton({ postId }) { const [liked, setLiked] = useState(false); return <button onClick={() => setLiked(!liked)}>♥</button> }

stages.name: What you can't do
stages.claim: no state, effects, handlers or browser APIs
stages.html:
Not in a Server Component Why
useState, useEffect, event handlers it doesn't run in the browser
browser APIs (window, localStorage) no browser on the server
useContext no client React tree there
passing functions as props to client components not serialisable (Server Actions excepted)

stages.name: So what for the system
stages.html: • Keep 'use client' boundaries low and small (leaves), pass serialisable data, fetch in Server Components in parallel, and be careful with secrets — anything passed to a Client Component is visible in the browser.

followUps.question: You put 'use client' at the top of the root layout. What happens to the app?
followUps.html: Everything imported below becomes client code: the RSC benefits (no server-only code in the bundle, server data access in components) are lost for the whole tree. Push the directive down to interactive leaves.

followUps.question: "RSC is just SSR."
followUps.html: SSR produces HTML for the first load, and components still hydrate and ship their code. RSC components never ship code or hydrate; they can be combined with SSR.

followUps.question: Can a Client Component render a Server Component?
followUps.html: Not by importing it; but a Server Component can pass another Server Component as children or a prop into a Client Component, and it's rendered on the server.

followUps.question: What's a security risk with RSC?
followUps.html: Accidentally passing sensitive fields (whole user records, tokens) as props to a Client Component, which serialises them into the payload. Select only what the client needs.

followUps.question: How would you use RSC in an AI product?
followUps.html: Server Components for conversation lists and history (fetched close to the data), Client Components for the composer and streaming view, and server-side calls to the LLM so keys stay on the server; stream partial UI with Suspense.

dontSay: 'use client' at the root by default.

react-q38.testing: why use is exempt from the hooks ordering rule, and what it needs around it.
react-q38.spoken:
"B: yes. use is allowed inside conditions and loops.

The reason normal hooks can't be conditional is that they own a slot in the component's hook list, matched by call order. use doesn't store state in a slot: it reads a value from a promise or a context. For a promise, if it's resolved, use returns the value; if it's pending, it suspends the component — React shows the nearest Suspense fallback and retries when the promise settles; if it rejected, it throws to the nearest error boundary.

So it needs a Suspense boundary and an error boundary above it, and the promise must be stable — created outside render, for example passed down from a Server Component or a cache — or every render creates a new promise and suspends forever."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
import { use } from 'react';
function Message({ promise }) {
  if (!promise) return <Empty />;
  const text = use(promise);
  return <p>{text}</p>;
}
  • A: No — it breaks the rules of hooks · B: Yes — use may be called conditionally and inside loops · C: Only inside a Server Component · D: Yes, but it throws unless wrapped in useMemo

stages.name: Trace the render
stages.html:
Prove it:

// <Suspense fallback={<p>loading</p>}><Message promise={null} /></Suspense>
// → "empty"
// same with promise = Promise.resolve('hello')
// → "hello"                   (React 19.3, jsdom harness)

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.claim: use reads, it doesn't own a slot
stages.html:
useState use(promise)
stores state in hook list yes no
can be conditional no yes
pending behaviour — suspends
rejected behaviour — throws to error boundary

stages.name: Variants that flip it
stages.claim: promises made in render never resolve
stages.html:
• use(fetch(url)) created in render → each retry creates a new pending promise → the component stays on the fallback (measured: still "loading" after 80 ms, React 19.3).
  • No Suspense boundary above → the root suspends; no error boundary → rejection crashes the tree.
  • use(Context) → reads context conditionally, an alternative to useContext.

stages.name: The production version
stages.html: • Start data fetching in a Server Component, pass the promise to a Client Component, and use it there under Suspense — streaming without a client fetch waterfall.

followUps.question: const text = use(fetch('/api/msg').then(r => r.text())) inside the component. What happens?
followUps.html: Each render creates a new promise, so the component suspends, retries with another new pending promise, and never shows the result — in the jsdom harness it was still on the fallback after 80 ms. Create the promise outside render (cache, parent, Server Component).

followUps.question: "use is a hook, so it can't be conditional."
followUps.html: It's called "use" but it doesn't depend on call order; React explicitly allows conditional and looped calls.

followUps.question: Is use only for Server Components?
followUps.html: No, it works in Client Components too; in Server Components you'd usually just await instead.

followUps.question: What happens when the promise rejects?
followUps.html: use throws the error; the nearest error boundary catches it and shows its fallback.

followUps.question: How does this change data fetching patterns?
followUps.html: It lets you start fetches early (server or route level) and read them late (in the component that needs the data), which removes effect-based fetching and waterfalls when combined with Suspense.

react-q39.testing: what hydration compares, and the environment differences localhost hides.
react-q39.spoken:
"Hydration means React on the client renders the same tree the server rendered and attaches to the existing HTML. A mismatch means the server's HTML and the client's first render disagreed. React 19 reports it with a diff of the mismatching text or attribute, so I start by reading that diff and the component stack in production logs, or reproduce with a production build locally.

Why production only? Because the differences that cause mismatches are ones localhost hides. Time: the server renders in UTC in another region, my laptop in my timezone, so a formatted date differs. Locale: toLocaleString differs between the server's Node locale and the user's browser. Non-determinism: Date.now(), Math.random() or generated IDs in render. Browser-only reads during render: window, localStorage, matchMedia — the server takes one branch, the client another. Feature flags or A/B assignments resolved differently on server and client. And things outside React: browser extensions or CDN/edge rewriting injecting markup, and cached HTML from an older deploy served with newer JavaScript.

Fixes by cause: make render deterministic — pass the timestamp or locale from the server, use useId for IDs; move browser-only values into an effect so the first client render matches the server, then update; evaluate flags once on the server and pass them down; and fix caching so HTML and JS versions match. suppressHydrationWarning only for genuinely unavoidable leaf text like a timestamp."

stages.name: Read the symptom
stages.html: • Errors in production logs; sometimes content flickers or React re-renders the whole root on the client.

stages.name: Measure before guessing
stages.claim: read the diff, reproduce with a prod build
stages.html: • React 19's error shows the mismatching text/attribute and component stack; run next build && next start with TZ=UTC and another locale to reproduce.

stages.name: Rank the suspects
stages.html:
Suspect Why prod-only
timezone/locale formatting server in UTC/other locale; laptop matches browser
Date.now(), Math.random(), ad-hoc IDs same machine hides timing differences less reliably
window/localStorage/matchMedia in render server branch ≠ client branch
feature flags / A/B different evaluation contexts
extensions, CDN/edge HTML rewriting not present locally
stale cached HTML vs new JS only after deploys

stages.name: Confirm
stages.html:
Prove it — the classic timezone mismatch and its fix:

// server (TZ=UTC) and browser (Asia/Kolkata) produce different text
function Posted({ iso }) { return <time>{new Date(iso).toLocaleString()}</time> }   // ❌ mismatch

function PostedFixed({ iso }) {
  const [text, setText] = useState(iso)                     // server and first client render agree
  useEffect(() => setText(new Date(iso).toLocaleString()), [iso])   // local format after hydration
  return <time dateTime={iso}>{text}</time>
}

stages.name: Fix
stages.html: • Deterministic inputs from the server (time, locale, flags); useId for IDs; browser-only values after mount; consistent HTML/JS versions (cache headers, deploy strategy).

stages.name: Guard against the next one
stages.claim: prod builds with a foreign timezone in CI
stages.html: • E2E tests against production builds with non-local TZ/locale; hydration errors reported to monitoring with release tags; lint for window access during render.

followUps.question: A component renders {typeof window === 'undefined' ? 'server' : 'client'}. What happens on hydration?
followUps.html: Mismatch: the server HTML says "server", the client's first render says "client". Render the same thing first and switch in an effect.

followUps.question: "Add suppressHydrationWarning."
followUps.html: It silences one level of text/attribute differences; the underlying bug remains elsewhere and the content can still be wrong. Use it only for unavoidable leaf values.

followUps.question: Why is a mismatch more than a warning?
followUps.html: React may discard server HTML and re-render on the client (slower, flicker), and event handlers can attach to the wrong elements if structure differs.

followUps.question: How can browser extensions cause it?
followUps.html: They modify the DOM before React hydrates (injecting attributes or elements). React 19 is more tolerant of some third-party insertions, but it's a known source of noise in logs.

followUps.question: How do deploys cause hydration errors?
followUps.html: A CDN serves cached HTML from version N while the browser loads JavaScript from N+1 (or the reverse). Version assets and HTML together, set cache headers correctly, and include the build ID in error reports.

react-q40.testing: what the compiler can and can't prove, and how review shifts to purity.
react-q40.trap: "memo is dead" or "the compiler fixes performance".
react-q40.spoken:
"Mostly redundant, not dead.

The React Compiler analyses components and hooks at build time and inserts memoization automatically — caching computed values, JSX and callbacks — at a finer grain than people write by hand. Where it applies, manual useMemo, useCallback and React.memo add nothing, and new code shouldn't need them.

But it only optimises what it can prove is safe: components that follow the Rules of React — pure render, props and state treated as immutable, hooks called unconditionally. If a component mutates a prop or reads a ref during render, the compiler skips it, and you get no memoization there at all. Manual memo still matters where you need a guaranteed stable reference for correctness — an effect dependency that must not change, or an identity a third-party library relies on — and in code the compiler bails out of.

So the review checklist moves from 'did you memoize this?' to 'is this component pure?': no mutation of props or state, no side effects or ref reads during render, correct dependency arrays, and the compiler's ESLint rules clean. And we check the compiler's output or the Profiler for components it skipped. Existing useMemo can stay; I remove it gradually where it's noise."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html: "The compiler removes most performance memoization; it doesn't remove the need for pure components."

stages.name: What the compiler takes over
stages.html: • Values, callbacks and JSX memoized per component, including cases humans rarely memoize (JSX subtrees, inline objects).

stages.name: Where manual memo remains
stages.html:
Case Why
compiler bailed out (impure code) no automatic memo
identity needed for correctness e.g. effect deps, external library caches
code outside the compiler's scope non-React modules, class components

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: can the compiler prove this component pure?
stages.html:
Prove it — a pattern the compiler must skip:

function Cart({ items }) {
  items.sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)       // ❌ mutates a prop during render
  return items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} />)
}
function CartFixed({ items }) {
  const sorted = [...items].sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)   // ✅ pure; compiler can memoize
  return sorted.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} />)
}

The first also has a real bug (mutating the parent's array); the compiler's lint flags this class of code.

stages.name: What changes in review
stages.html: • Purity over memo: no prop/state mutation, no side effects or ref reads in render, rules of hooks, compiler lint clean; manual memo only with a stated reason.

followUps.question: With the compiler on, a component passes style={{ color: 'red' }} to a child. Does the child re-render on every parent render?
followUps.html: Typically no: the compiler memoizes the object literal and the JSX, so the child receives the same props and can skip. Without the compiler it would re-render (Q17).

followUps.question: "The compiler fixes React performance."
followUps.html: It removes unnecessary re-renders; it doesn't fix expensive single renders, huge DOM, waterfalls or bundle size.

followUps.question: Should we delete all existing useMemo/useCallback?
followUps.html: Not in a big bang; they're harmless. Remove where they add noise, keep where identity matters for correctness, and verify with tests.

followUps.question: How do you adopt it safely?
followUps.html: Enable the ESLint rules first, fix violations, turn the compiler on per directory or by opt-in, and compare behaviour and Profiler results.

followUps.question: What does this mean for hiring and code style?
followUps.html: Less time on memo tricks, more on correct data flow and pure components — the skills that also make concurrent rendering and Server Components work.

links.label: AR4 Living with a Fast Moving Framework

react-q41.testing: rendering as early as correctness and personalisation allow.
react-q41.spoken:
"My rule: render as early as correctness allows. The earlier HTML is produced — build time rather than request time rather than in the browser — the faster and cheaper it is, as long as the content is still correct for the person seeing it.

Docs site: static generation. The content changes when someone publishes, not per user; build it once, serve it from the CDN, rebuild or revalidate on publish. Fastest possible and nearly free to serve.

E-commerce category page: incremental static regeneration. It needs SEO and fast loads, so it should be pre-rendered HTML, but prices and stock change during the day. ISR serves a cached static page and regenerates it in the background after a time window or on demand when the catalogue changes. Per-user parts — cart count, personalised recommendations — load on the client or stream in separately, so the main page stays cacheable.

Logged-in dashboard: client rendering of the data, inside a server-rendered or static shell. The content is per user, so it can't be cached at the CDN, and it doesn't need SEO. With the App Router I'd render the shell and layout on the server, stream user data through Server Components where it helps first load, and use a client query cache for the live, interactive parts.

In the App Router these are per-route and even per-component choices, not app-wide modes."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
Strategy HTML made Good for
SSG build content that changes on publish
ISR build + background regeneration public pages with changing data
SSR each request personalised or real-time pages needing SEO/first paint
CSR in the browser private, interactive, no SEO

stages.name: The docs site
stages.html: • CDN-served, revalidate on publish (webhook), versioned URLs.

stages.name: The category page
stages.html:
Prove it — App Router ISR:

// app/c/[slug]/page.jsx
export const revalidate = 300                       // regenerate at most every 5 minutes
export default async function Category({ params }) {
  const { slug } = await params
  const products = await getProducts(slug)          // cached with the page
  return <ProductGrid products={products} />        // cart badge is a client component
}
// on catalogue change: revalidatePath(`/c/${slug}`) from a webhook for immediate refresh

stages.name: The dashboard
stages.claim: CSR data in a server shell
stages.html: • Auth-gated, per-user, no SEO; shell/layout from the server, data via Server Components or client queries, live updates client-side.

stages.name: What I'd pick and revisit
stages.html: • Revisit if: prices must be exact per request (SSR or client price fetch), docs become per-customer (SSR/auth), dashboard needs shareable public views (SSR/ISR for those).

followUps.question: With ISR revalidate = 300, a price changes at 10:00:10. The page was generated at 10:00:00. When does a visitor see the new price?
followUps.html: After the window passes (10:05:00): the first request after that gets the stale page and triggers regeneration; the next request sees the new price — unless you call revalidatePath on change for immediate refresh. For exact checkout prices, re-check on the server at add-to-cart.

followUps.question: "SSR everything for SEO."
followUps.html: Static/ISR pages are equally indexable and much cheaper and faster; SSR is for content that must be computed per request.

followUps.question: Why not CSR for the category page?
followUps.html: Worse LCP and SEO: users and crawlers get an empty shell and wait for JavaScript and API calls.

followUps.question: Where does streaming fit?
followUps.html: SSR with Suspense can send the shell immediately and stream slower sections, improving TTFB and LCP for dynamic pages.

followUps.question: How do you keep a mostly static page personalised?
followUps.html: Keep the page static/ISR and load personalised fragments separately — client components or streamed server components — so the CDN-cached HTML stays shared across users.

dontSay: One rendering mode for the whole app.

react-q42.testing: an org-structure solution with real runtime costs, and the cheaper alternative.
react-q42.spoken:
"Micro-frontends buy one thing: independent deployment for independent teams. Each team builds, tests and releases its slice of the UI on its own schedule, possibly with its own stack.

They cost you at runtime and in coordination. Duplicated dependencies unless you share them carefully — two copies of React is both bigger and broken for hooks — so shared-dependency versioning becomes a cross-team negotiation. Shared state and routing across slices get awkward. Design consistency needs a shared design system that everyone upgrades. And performance has no single owner: each slice adds its JavaScript, and nobody owns the page's LCP or INP.

So they're worth it when the release process is genuinely the bottleneck: many teams — say more than five or six — on one product surface, blocked by a single release train, with domains that split cleanly, like account, checkout and search, or when integrating acquired apps built on other stacks.

Otherwise a monorepo with enforced module boundaries — ownership via CODEOWNERS, lint rules on imports, per-package builds and tests — gives most of the team autonomy with one runtime and one deployment."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: deploy independence vs runtime and coordination cost
stages.html: "Micro-frontends are an organisational tool with technical costs."

stages.name: Where micro-frontends win
stages.claim: many teams, clean seams, mixed stacks
stages.html: • Many teams blocked on one release train; clean domain seams; mixed stacks (acquisitions, legacy migration via strangler).

stages.name: Where a modular monolith wins
stages.html:
Prove it — boundaries without separate runtimes:

// eslint: packages may only import each other's public entry points
'no-restricted-imports': ['error', { patterns: ['@app/checkout/src/*', '@app/search/src/*'] }]
// CODEOWNERS: /packages/checkout/ @team-checkout
Micro-frontends Modular monorepo
independent deploys yes per app, shared release
runtime duplication risk high none
shared state/routing hard normal
performance ownership fragmented single

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: is the release train the bottleneck?
stages.html: • Measure lead time and deploy blocking; if teams mainly suffer from code coupling, boundaries fix it without a runtime split.

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.html: • Modular monorepo by default; micro-frontends (Module Federation or route-level composition) only for clear domain seams and team scale, with a shared design system and a performance budget per slice.

followUps.question: 🧪 Two micro-frontends each bundle their own React 19 copy and share a component that uses hooks. What happens?
followUps.html: "Invalid hook call" errors or broken context: two React copies don't share internal state. Share React as a singleton via Module Federation or externals.

followUps.question: "Micro-frontends improve performance."
followUps.html: Usually the opposite: more JavaScript, duplicated libraries, extra requests. They improve team independence.

followUps.question: What are the composition options?
followUps.html: Route-level (separate apps per path behind a proxy), build-time packages (not truly independent), runtime composition (Module Federation, web components), and server-side composition (edge includes).

followUps.question: How do you keep design consistent?
followUps.html: A versioned design system with tokens, visual regression tests, and an upgrade policy — or it drifts slice by slice.

followUps.question: How would you migrate a legacy app with micro-frontends?
followUps.html: As a strangler: route new sections to a new app behind the same domain, share auth and a shell, move routes over one by one, and retire the old app — then decide whether to stay split.

dontSay: Adopting them for code organisation alone.

react-q43.testing: testing observable behaviour, the integration-heavy shape, and keeping e2e small.
react-q43.trap: snapshot tests and implementation-detail tests as the strategy.
react-q43.spoken:
"I test what the user can observe, and I put most of the effort where confidence per cost is highest.

Unit tests for pure logic: reducers, formatters, validation, data transforms, custom hooks with tricky logic. Fast and precise.

The bulk goes to integration tests: render a feature — a form, a search page — with React Testing Library, interact the way a user does, by role and label, and assert what they'd see. The network is mocked at the boundary with MSW, so the real data-fetching code, query cache and error handling run; only the server is fake. These catch most bugs and survive refactors because they don't depend on implementation details.

A small, deliberate set of end-to-end tests with Playwright on the flows that lose money or trust if broken: sign-in, checkout, the core AI chat send-and-stream. Run against a production-like build, with stable test data.

Around that: type checking and lint as the cheapest layer, accessibility checks in integration tests, visual regression for the design system, and contract tests or generated types for the API.

I avoid snapshot tests of whole components and tests that assert on state or internals — they break on every refactor and catch little."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Money flows, auth, data loss, core product loop (e.g. chat send). Those get e2e.

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • CI time budget; e2e flakiness grows with count; tests must survive refactors.

stages.name: Baseline strategy
stages.html:
Layer What Tools
static types, lint, hooks rules TypeScript, ESLint
unit pure logic, reducers, hooks Vitest/Jest
integration (bulk) features through the UI, network mocked RTL + MSW
e2e (few) critical journeys on real build Playwright
extra a11y, visual regression, contract axe, Chromatic/Playwright screenshots, OpenAPI types

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Prove it:

server.use(http.get('/api/search', () => HttpResponse.json([{ id: 1, title: 'React hooks' }])))
test('shows results for a query', async () => {
  render(<SearchPage />, { wrapper: QueryProvider })
  await userEvent.type(screen.getByRole('searchbox', { name: /search/i }), 'hooks')
  expect(await screen.findByRole('link', { name: 'React hooks' })).toBeInTheDocument()
})

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Snapshot sprawl; testing internals (state, class names); mocking modules instead of the network; many flaky e2e tests; no tests for error and loading states.

stages.name: What I'd measure
stages.html: • Escaped defects by layer, CI time, flake rate for e2e, and coverage of critical flows (not line coverage percentages).

followUps.question: A test finds a button with container.querySelector('.btn-primary'). You rename the CSS class. What happens?
followUps.html: The test breaks though behaviour didn't change. getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }) survives refactors and checks accessibility at the same time.

followUps.question: "100% coverage with snapshot tests."
followUps.html: Snapshots record output without asserting intent; people update them blindly. Coverage percentage says little about catching bugs.

followUps.question: Why MSW over mocking fetch in each test?
followUps.html: It intercepts at the network layer, so real fetching code, caching and error handling run, and the same handlers work in tests, Storybook and local dev.

followUps.question: How do you test streaming UIs?
followUps.html: MSW can return a ReadableStream; assert progressive rendering with findBy queries, and test abort/retry paths. E2E covers one real streaming flow.

followUps.question: How do you keep e2e fast and reliable?
followUps.html: Few tests on critical paths, isolated test data per run, API setup instead of UI setup, retries only with tracking of flake rates, and parallel sharding.

react-q44.testing: treating the request as a symptom, then a time-boxed, documented decision with boundaries.
react-q44.spoken:
"I start by asking what they can't do today. A request for a new library is usually a symptom: slow re-renders from context, boilerplate in server-data slices, or a missing pattern in the existing tools. Often the answer is using what we have correctly — server data in the query cache, selectors in the existing store — and the new library isn't needed.

If the need is real, it goes through a process, not a pull request. A time-boxed spike on one real feature, compared against the existing option on the criteria that matter: the problem it solves, bundle size, learning cost, testing, devtools, maintenance and community health. Then a short ADR — the architecture decision record — stating the decision, the alternatives, and the adoption boundary: which categories of state it's for and which it isn't.

And crucially a deprecation plan: if it overlaps with an existing library, which one goes away, and how we migrate, so we don't end up with four libraries holding overlapping state. The ADR, a reference implementation and lint rules make the boundary stick."

stages.name: Clarify the need
stages.html:
Stated need Likely real cause Existing fix
"Context is slow" high-frequency state in context store with selectors
"Redux boilerplate" server data in Redux query library
"state everywhere" no state rules rules + migration (Q28)

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html: • Bundle, onboarding, patterns to maintain, overlapping mental models, upgrade burden.

stages.name: Baseline process
Deep-dive
stages.html:
Prove it — the spike scorecard (cells to fill):

Criterion Existing option Proposed library
solves the stated problem (demo) measure measure
bundle size (gzipped) measure measure
re-renders for the key interaction measure measure
test ergonomics / devtools assess assess
maintenance and community assess assess
migration cost — estimate

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html: • Libraries added per team without boundaries; overlapping state in several stores; no owner for removal; decisions made in PRs without a record.

stages.name: What I'd measure
stages.claim: fewer libraries, the problem metric improved
stages.html: • Number of state libraries in use, duplicated state sources, and after adoption, whether the stated problem metric (re-renders, boilerplate, bugs) improved.

followUps.question: 🧪 The spike shows the new library cuts re-renders on one screen from 40 to 5. The existing Zustand store with proper selectors gets 6. Decision?
followUps.html: Keep Zustand: the difference is negligible and a fourth library adds cost. Document the selector pattern so other teams get the same result.

followUps.question: "Just let teams choose their own libraries."
followUps.html: Autonomy without boundaries produces overlapping state and many patterns to maintain. Give choice within an agreed set.

followUps.question: What's in an ADR?
followUps.html: Context, the decision, alternatives considered, consequences, and the scope/boundary — short, dated and linked from the code.

followUps.question: How do you enforce the boundary?
followUps.html: Lint import rules for where the library may be used, a reference implementation, and review checklists.

followUps.question: How do you say no without killing morale?
followUps.html: Take the underlying problem seriously, fix it with existing tools together, and keep a clear, fair path for proposals backed by a spike — so the answer is about evidence, not authority.

dontSay: A decision without a deprecation plan.

react-q45.testing: render budget under streaming, runs that outlive the page, unpredictable output, and security.
react-q45.trap: setState per token into global state, and a fetch that dies with the tab.
react-q45.spoken:
"Three assumptions of a normal React app break.

The render budget: tokens can arrive faster than frames. If every token calls setState high in the tree — or in a global store — the whole transcript re-renders dozens of times a second, markdown is re-parsed each time, and typing lags. So I buffer incoming chunks in a ref and flush them to state once per animation frame, into an isolated leaf component for the streaming message only. Completed messages are memoized and never re-render; heavy markdown and code highlighting run deferred.

Request and response: an agent run can take minutes, and it outlives the page — the user refreshes, switches tabs or loses the network. So runs are server-owned and addressable by ID: the client starts a run and gets an ID, subscribes to its event stream via SSE, and can reconnect with the last event ID to resume. The run continues on the server whether or not anyone watches.

Optimistic UI: I can't predict the output, so instead I show honest progress — a run status state machine: queued, thinking, calling a tool, streaming, done, failed, cancelled — and a trace view of tool calls with their inputs and outputs, collapsed by default.

Around that: the transcript is server state, in the query cache, with the active stream merged in; cancel is a first-class action that aborts the server run; model output is untrusted, so markdown is sanitised, links are checked and no raw HTML is executed; and API keys stay on the server, behind a proxy with per-user rate limits."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html: • Token streaming, multi-minute agent runs with tool calls, cancellation, reconnect/resume, multi-tab, errors mid-stream.

stages.name: What breaks
stages.html:
Assumption Breaks because Design
render per state change is cheap tokens > frames buffer + rAF flush into a leaf
request/response runs outlive the page server-owned runs, resumable streams by ID
optimistic UI output unknowable status state machine + trace

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.claim: server-owned runs, buffered leaf, query cache

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
Prove it — buffer tokens, flush once per frame:

function useTokenStream(runId) {
  const [text, setText] = useState('')
  const buf = useRef('')
  useEffect(() => {
    const es = new EventSource(`/api/runs/${runId}/events`)
    let raf = 0
    es.onmessage = e => {
      buf.current += JSON.parse(e.data).t
      raf ||= requestAnimationFrame(() => { const chunk = buf.current; buf.current = ''; raf = 0; setText(t => t + chunk) })
    }
    return () => { es.close(); cancelAnimationFrame(raf) }
  }, [runId])
  return text
}
// read the buffer before clearing it: `setText(t => t + buf.current)` runs later and would see ''
// simulated 100 tokens over 10 frames (React 19.3, jsdom harness):
// → lazy read:  50 of 100 chars shown (tokens lost)
// → read first: 100 of 100 chars, 10 flushes for 10 frames

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.claim: per-token global updates and tab-bound runs
stages.html: • Global store updated per token; stream tied to the tab (lost on refresh); cancel only stops the UI, not the server run (still billed); unsanitised markdown (XSS via model output); keys in the browser.

stages.name: What I'd monitor
stages.html: • TTFT in the browser, frames dropped while streaming, INP of send/cancel, reconnect success rate, runs cancelled vs completed, and client errors per run ID.

followUps.question: Tokens arrive at 200/s and each calls setMessages in a global store read by 30 components. What happens?
followUps.html: Up to 200 store updates per second, each re-rendering every subscriber and re-parsing markdown: dropped frames and laggy input. Buffer per frame and confine updates to the streaming leaf.

followUps.question: "Just use the AI SDK's useChat and you're done."
followUps.html: It solves streaming for simple chats. Long-running agent runs, resumability, multi-tab and traces still need server-owned runs and state design around it.

followUps.question: SSE or WebSockets?
followUps.html: SSE for server-to-client token/event streams (simple, resumable with Last-Event-ID); WebSockets when the client must send mid-run (interrupts, voice).

followUps.question: How do you render model markdown safely?
followUps.html: A markdown renderer without raw HTML (or sanitised with DOMPurify), link allow-listing or warnings, and no auto-loading of external images, which can exfiltrate data.

followUps.question: The user closes the tab mid-run and comes back later. What do they see?
followUps.html: The run continued server-side; reopening the conversation loads the transcript from the query cache and, if the run is still active, re-subscribes from the last event ID; if finished, the final message is simply there.

dontSay: Runs tied to the browser tab.
